IMPRIMATUR

From the Vicariate of Rome

Fr. Luigi Moretti

Secretary General

© Congregation of the Daughters of Saint Anne - Via Merulana, 177 - 00185 ROME

The title of this biography of Fr. Giovanni Battista Tornatore reflects the concern of the modern reader of biographies of saints or of other significant figures of a historical period: not a search for the sensational, but a documented reading of a life open to an ideal, embraced perhaps in suffering and struggle, yet carried out in the deep consistency of everyday life.

Fr. Tornatore is one of these figures. He lived and long remained in the shadow of a minor city, Piacenza, known by his contemporaries as a “saint” for his way of life, his commitment to study and prayer, and the soundness and richness of his spiritual direction. His was a holiness appreciated above all because it was simple, hidden, shunning any desire to be noticed. It reflected the characteristic virtues of the spirit of the founder of his religious Congregation, Saint Vincent de Paul, from whom he had inherited love for the service of God on behalf of the poor and the clergy.

He is described to us as a figure austere with himself but sensitive toward others, deeply devoted to the study of the ecclesiastical sciences, which he taught for many years at the Alberoni College, yet not cut off from reality and from living problems, able to penetrate the situations and the spirit of those who turned to him for spiritual accompaniment.

What characterizes Tornatore’s life, together with study and learning, is his collaboration with Mother Rosa Gattorno. Their first meeting was by chance, as often happens in the works of God. But both gradually understood that they had been chosen as instruments for the fulfilment of a single mission of grace. From their insights, from their mutual knowledge and esteem, from the soundness of their spiritual life and their love for the Church, the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne came to life and became established.

The life, hopes and ideals of Mother Rosa and Fr. Tornatore became ever more deeply identified with the vicissitudes of the new institution which, like all the works of God, had been born and was growing stronger amid inevitable difficulties and misunderstandings. The pages of this biography rightly dwell on the relationship of work and consecration of both of them to the life of the new family. In it the sense of motherhood and fatherhood grows stronger and is expressed ever more clearly, through spiritual and material concerns and anxious care for the first steps of a still fragile creature.

The spiritually most significant page of this collaboration (amply presented in this biography) is the long story of the Rules of the Institute. Entrusted to Fr. Tornatore to prepare and approved by the Bishop of Piacenza, after a long wait they were instead rejected by the Roman authorities. In them Tornatore had expressed the richness of his mystical spirit, an attention to spiritual values more than to juridical details, and the communication of a deep spirit of service to God and to the poor. But the form was not suited to the times, faithful to a formal tradition and certainly not yet open to true “novelties”. The rejection of the text was made heavier still by the order to remove Tornatore from any spiritual or governing role in the Institute. Unfounded accusations of false mysticism had been added to equally unjust accusations concerning his philosophical and theological teaching, as happened to many other significant figures of the time. The moral suffering was accepted and borne in exemplary silence, painful but full of hope that these misfortunes would not halt the progress of God’s work. It was the merit of Bishop Scalabrini to resolve the problem with his bold heart, open to new horizons.

Tornatore’s notes on this affair, reproduced in the biography, reveal the whole wound of seeing himself deprived of recognition of his fatherhood of the Institute. But they also show him to us in the richness of his life of faith and of abandonment into the hands of divine Providence. A true human and spiritual greatness shines through them, the fruit of a deep and prolonged experience of God.

Fr. Tornatore found the strength for this endurance under trial in faith, sustained by constant and convinced prayer. The biography reveals his deep love for the Eucharist and for the fundamental mysteries of the Trinity and the Incarnation, and his simple but heartfelt devotion to Mary and to her mother Saint Anne, whom he sees as the type of a new spirituality in the Church, that of the poor of Yahweh who await and serve the fulfilment of the Kingdom of God. He admires Saint Anne at the summit of God’s whole plan, to which she gave her collaboration. Thus she becomes the type of a new form of following Christ in the Church.

The rediscovery of the figure of Fr. Tornatore seems to me significant and fruitful: he is a mystic, a man of great spiritual experience, the promoter of a new charism in the following of Christ in the Church, learned and versatile in the ecclesiastical and human sciences. He is a man of faith and charity who still has a message to communicate. We need such figures to recover many fundamental values of the Gospel.

But certainly more significant is the rediscovery of the figure of Fr. Tornatore and of his spirituality by the Daughters of Saint Anne. When Tornatore’s mortal remains were transferred to their Mother House in 1981, they spoke of a “return of the Father”. It was not only a material return. This biography shows their journey of spiritual rediscovery of the one who was a father of the Institute through the help he gave the Foundress in identifying the spirit of the foundation. The Council’s call to return to the sources led their General Chapters to rediscover the importance of Fr. Tornatore’s presence beside Mother Rosa at the origins of their Institute. Providence led them to rediscover their genuine spirit “in the attitude of poverty of heart and motherly dedication that was proper to Saint Anne”, which expresses the charism and spirituality of Mother Rosa as set out by Fr. Tornatore in the Rules of 1869.

This biography appears on the occasion of the centenary of the Father’s death. It is the first attempt at a fairly broad and complete biography, beyond the short profiles published from time to time and some rather thematic presentations in the magazines of the Daughters of Saint Anne and of the Priests of the Mission. Thanks to the Author for the work he has done in illustrating the life of Fr. Tornatore, interwoven with that of Mother Rosa, become a wish for the Daughters of Saint Anne: that they not reduce the anniversary to a mere historical commemoration, one of the many that flourish in our day, but make it a further stimulus to research into and deeper understanding of the values and strength of their origins.

Fr. Carlo Braga, C.M.

To read Christian existence is to adore God, Creator and Lord of the universe; it is a hymn of praise, a contemplation of the ineffable mystery of the Holy Trinity that unfolds in history and becomes visible in human persons.

The Father reveals in his Son the plan of infinite love and goodness; Christ casts the divine light upon the human face; the Spirit brings the plan of salvation to fulfilment. In this perspective it is possible to read the enigmas of history and to find some explanation of the human story.

Father Giovanni Battista Tornatore, a Vincentian religious and priest who lived between Rome and Piacenza from 1820 to 1895, must therefore be approached in the light of the very mystery of God: his existence can be explained only in relation to the Person of the Living God. Every vocation, after all, can be read only starting from God and from his saving plan.

This biography has therefore been written in the awareness that the Lord stands at the basis of every discourse about the human person and his vocation, since it is God who opens the dialogue of love and points out the way to follow. On this journey man has Christ as companion, God as Father, Mary as Mother, and the Church as the place where the Mystery of salvation takes shape. Fr. Tornatore fully embodies Jesus the Redeemer through his baptismal consecration, the Sequela Christi (= the following of Christ), and the utopia of the Beatitudes within a specific charism.

The Spirit completes the work of salvation begun by Christ and with his gifts offers the possibility of returning to the Father and of bringing the good news of the Gospel to fulfilment.

Thus Fr. Giovanni Battista Tornatore reveals in his life the very mystery of God and the mystery of Christ through being united with his death and resurrection. Fr. Tornatore’s existence makes clear (but only now, that is, in hindsight!) the thread of Providence that surrounds and involves his person.

From this point of view the biographer’s task is particularly arduous! It is a matter of making manifest the very mystery of God present in Father Tornatore; of illustrating the work he accomplished in the last century and gathering the messages he handed on. A life and messages bound up with light and shadow, with inspiring projects and complex situations, often difficult to interpret if not humanly incomprehensible. We stand before a figure truly rich in qualities and talents, perceptive and guided by supernatural action. Fr. Tornatore built up the Church by his religious profession, his life, his writings, his witness and therefore his spirituality, which is typically martyrial in nature.

A shining beacon in the second half of the last century, he takes his place among eminent figures such as Frassinetti, Cottolengo, John Bosco, Benedetto Dusmet and others, and hands on to history a great heritage of culture and holiness. For this reason Fr. Tornatore is still today a stimulus for the conscience of the ecclesial community and a point of reference for the people of yesterday and of our time.

A valuable collaborator of Mother Rosa and of her work, he is counselor and guide for the newborn Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne.

He promotes its charism by formulating its spiritual doctrine and works hard for its spread.

This collaboration is deeply marked by the mystery of the Cross and of suffering, which Tornatore took up as his example and model of life. One more reason to approach him on tiptoe, aware of grasping only a few glimmers of the immense light surrounding his life, in order to find some signs that are milestones of his particular journey.

This is therefore an unusual biography, drawn up on the basis of the sources and authentic documentation, built from significant pieces and from small essential pictures that construct the figure, sketch the person and bring his image into focus.

A simple text with a sapiential character, intended to bring out the theological and spiritual content so abundantly present in Tornatore’s personality. This small contribution would also like to offer a cross-section of the work of the Priest of the Mission, examined from different angles and in the style, now very widespread, of concentric circles! Obviously the research does not come from nothing: the careful studies of some Daughters of Saint Anne, as well as of Fiocchi, Barra, Iriarte, Rossi, Francesconi, Manfredini and other able researchers, are its foundation and essential point of reference.

To all this must be added the remarkable effort made by the Institute after the Council, with its immense output aimed at bringing the charism into focus in its dynamic development as well as in its origin.

Seen in this perspective, the present work aims to offer a word of life and therefore a help toward guiding the Christian community of our day.

A deeper study of Mother Rosa’s charism leads back to the work of the Priest of the Mission; to the travail and the good fight fought by both for love of Christ; to humble and constant faithfulness to the appointments written in God’s plan and accepted in faith; to their sense of the Church and their communion with the Bishop: these are some significant stages of this publication, which was requested of me by the Mother General, Mother Virginia Sinagra, and her council.

Fr. Tornatore is alive and still speaks... and the Church of every age will have to listen to his voice and treasure his teaching, his experience and his passion for Christ and for souls. When God raises up people like Fr. Tornatore, it is not so much that we may talk about him as that we may take up his legacy.

P. Giovanni Battista Tornatore

At only 16, drawn by the missionary ideal, Tornatore entered the Congregation of the Priests of the Mission in 1836. From 1844 he was assigned to the direction of students and to teaching. He was professor of moral theology and sacred scripture for very many years at the famous college.

a. Biographical notes

Giovanni Battista Tornatore was born to Bartolomeo and Rosa Campana in Dolceacqua, in the diocese of Ventimiglia, on 11 April 1820. He was a healthy and promising boy, brought up in an ordinary family, God-fearing and committed to giving their children bread, education and religious faith. Early on, his brother Domenico received the gift of a vocation and set out on the religious and priestly life with the Lazarist Fathers, or Priests of the Mission, who since the time of Saint Vincent de Paul had spread their charism in France, Italy and other European countries. In Rome a prestigious house known as Montecitorio had been founded in 1642. It was here, in this Institute, that Giovanni Battista Tornatore went on 20 December 1836, at the age of 16, to visit his brother. Won over by the welcome of the Fathers and by his brother’s happiness, and above all captivated by the life lived there, he decided to enter that house and embrace that way of life.

Entrusted to the care of the Novice Master, Fr. Leonardo Pellegrini, a religious of deep interior life and rather strict in observing the rule of Saint Vincent, Tornatore made progress on the way of perfection. Having then passed the scrutiny, he was admitted to religious profession.

Meanwhile the novice Tornatore came to know all the harsh and hard things through which one goes to God, and was initiated into truly seeking the Lord by offering him his first service, into practizing prompt and joyful obedience, and into bearing the inevitable frictions that come from living together. He experienced community life and so tasted both the beauty of communion and the wounds of division! Religious life is indeed a marvel of the Spirit, a mystery that involves joy and resurrection together with suffering and the cross: it is the mystery of Christ, living and vibrant! Tornatore became aware of all this and every day responded positively to the call of the Spirit, who wanted him to be a true and authentic Vincentian.

But meanwhile he had to build his personality by knowing himself well: his genetic make-up, his temperament, his character, his passions, his sensitivity, his feelings, his inclinations, his intelligence, the way he related to others, his qualities of mind and heart as well as his weaknesses; in a word, he had to become aware of his personality profile. This is indeed a basic condition for then developing a serious plan of Christian and religious life.

b. Personality profile

In the light of his numerous publications, his many-sided activities and the way he “managed” his Christian and religious vocation, a rather complex and very significant personality emerges.

Gifted with great insight, Fr. Tornatore embarked on creative paths, which he pursued with practicality and dedication.

A lover of philosophy, he was able to act according to criteria of balanced discernment and objective judgment.

Deeply imbued with his “call” among the priests of the Mission, Fr. Tornatore lived his consecration in the depths of his being, and as such, that is as a “religious”, he showed himself to everyone and in every circumstance.

He was passionate about the search for truth and freedom, which he nevertheless combined harmoniously with self-mastery, self-control and asceticism, and also with the order, discipline and “style” of his Institute.

In the various circumstances of his life Father Tornatore showed great sensitivity and attention, especially toward the destitute and needy, and worked with all his strength to relieve suffering, to support others, and so to offer the poor real relief and help.

His altruistic impulses and remarkable generosity fed plans marked by prophecy and therefore by a drive toward the new, which he nonetheless managed to bring back within the bounds of obedience and authority. Emblematic in this respect would be his experience in the field of studies (see above all the accusations of being a Rosminian sympathizer!) and later his exclusion from the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne.

Even in difficult situations Fr. Tornatore did not lose his usual calm and serenity of spirit; he showed compliance and sought in his inner life and in faith the light needed to overcome the problem and go on living in peace.

Particularly attentive to the heritage and style of his Institute, Fr. Tornatore fully lived out the spiritual formation that had gradually shaped him and moved toward the goal to which he had been directed. Hence his vital experience of prayer, which literally structured his life, tempered his character, fed his strength and strengthened his passion for the cause of the Gospel and for the good of the community. His sense of the Church should also be noted, which in him became prominent and took on ever greater space and ever wider horizons.

His weaknesses, such as pessimism, scrupulosity, anger and discouragement, found an antidote within his own person, in his positive qualities: openness, self-giving, charity, humility, service, availability to God, to his superiors, to the needs of the Church and above all to the action of the Spirit.

We thus have a person who was deeply human and at the same time deeply enlightened by grace, moving decisively toward the maturity of Christ.

In this respect Fr. Tornatore was a personality who faced everything with great seriousness and let himself be wholly involved in the new choice of life he had made. A companion of his in the novitiate and student house, a certain Berardi, noted Tornatore’s radical change after a course of spiritual exercises in preparation for Holy Easter.

Sharing in the Mystery of Christ would make him a sentinel of God, a man committed to the study of theology in highly scientific terms and at the same time open to reading and understanding the human family at a sacramental level.

Because of all this Fr. Tornatore became a clear point of reference and spoke a particularly incisive word in the Church and in history, one that left its mark.

c. A formation marked by simplicity

The formation of young men was in some way well tested. Saint Vincent had given fairly precise guidelines for all who wished to follow in his footsteps and embody his charism. The Saint pointed everyone to the way of simplicity, rich in an admirable life-giving power, to lead souls to perfection. Simplicity means sine plica (= without a fold), that is, straightforwardness together with clarity. Away, then, with artificial ways that lead to hypocrisy and to the rejection of the Gospel message; and instead openness and availability to Christ, to be taught by him, and to others, to welcome all that is positive in them.

Simplicity, in Saint Vincent’s thought and method and above all in his example, is trusting and serene abandonment to God’s Providence; full, conscious and joyful conformity to his will; filial trust in his dispositions, always admirable, always fatherly, always wise, which need neither our suggestions nor our pushing. Never to run ahead of the designs of Providence, but to follow them and, once they are known, to cooperate with them enthusiastically and with full dedication: this is a great principle of Vincentian teaching.

For Saint Vincent simplicity is also recognition of and homage to the authority of the Church and of the Pope in doctrine, government and ecclesiastical discipline; without hidden meanings or mental reservations; with sincerity and loyalty; because this is order. For each person it means staying in one’s own place, without false ambitions or apparent modesty; it means doing one’s duty with uprightness of heart, full awareness and a deep sense of responsibility, since the realization of God’s plan in us, in souls and in the Church depends on our fidelity and loyalty. To know how to guide ourselves, according to the rule and the will of our Superiors, yet as if neither existed outside us: here is another Vincentian principle of self-government and self-formation that flows from simplicity.

For Saint Vincent simplicity also excludes vanity, the craving for and pursuit of novelty for its own sake or for our vainglory; instead it gratefully receives and values the good and the results achieved in the past by those, students or superiors, who went before us: precious traditions rich in lessons for the future. Simplicity is cordiality in daily relationships, because it walks the straight paths of charity and love; it is the doing of good works and the giving of good example, because it prefers sincerity in action to disquisitions and controversies.

It is precisely along these lines of simplicity that the direction of Saint Vincent’s activity moves, «ad salutem pauperum» (= for the salvation of the poor) and «ad cleri disciplinam» (= for the discipline of the clergy).1 The Vincentian method relies heavily on this quality or virtue, to the point of making it an integral part of its charism and of its particular way of reading the Gospel, that is, of its spirituality.

d. The setting of Vincentian spirituality

Various elements and even schools of spirituality influenced both the formation of Vincent de Paul and his substantial teaching on the subject. The thought of Cardinal Bérulle, to whose direction Vincent entrusted himself for over a decade, the devout humanism of Saint Francis de Sales, his great friend, and Ignatian asceticism, to which Vincent was particularly drawn given his temperament, were decisive for his spiritual stature and for carrying out his particular project.

Vincent’s spiritual teaching must therefore be traced back to these three sources. Substantially, however, he remained a moralist, an ascetic, not a mystic. He transformed the contemplative imprint of Bérulle and Francis de Sales and, tempering it with Ignatian asceticism, worked out, without intending to, a new spiritual doctrine. The Vincentian draws his spiritual strength from morning meditation and from conformity to God’s will, but then turns wholly to the practice of the virtues of which Jesus Christ, the incarnate Son of God, has given us the example. It is precisely the scheme of the virtues, with its double value as God’s gift and man’s task, that shapes the spiritual journey. The characteristic virtues of the Vincentian spirit are, says the Rule of the Missionaries, the five stones of David: simplicity, humility, meekness, mortification and zeal for the salvation of souls. These five virtues, Vincent says, must be like the faculties of the soul of the whole Congregation.2

e. Field of action

Vincent’s specific field of action was charity, exercised according to criteria of relief, liberation and assistance, and with the chief aim of acting as mercy and compassion dictate.

Hence his work for the galley slaves, the prisoners waiting to be put aboard the king’s galleys as oarsmen. Vincent saw the wretched state of these brothers, was horrified, felt compassion for them and at once became their comforter and advocate.

“When I praised their resignation,” he later said, “when I pitied their sufferings... when I kissed their chains... then they listened to me.” Tradition, to underline better how Vincent shared the lot of these galley slaves, even portrayed him taking upon himself the chains of a convict.

Vincent came to the aid of the slaves of Barbary and took care of the foundlings, whom society hypocritically and contemptuously called the children of sin. To this end he set up the so-called “Vincentian associations” to look after an ever greater number of these children (there is even talk of 395 foundlings cared for).

Besides this, he considered it his duty to intervene to ensure a presence and assistance in the regions devastated by war. As a result of the Thirty Years’ War and of the various factions of the Fronde, many towns had been completely laid waste. So Vincent hurried to the aid of these distant places and organized in Paris centers for collecting relief in money and in kind, which his missionaries and sisters then took to their destination.

He also made use of the collaboration of the Company of the Blessed Sacrament. Made up of distinguished clergy and laity, its program was “every form of good”.

It is along these lines that the formation of young Vincentians proceeds.

A fairly demanding and scientifically sound intellectual formation. Direct contact above all with certain texts of Sacred Scripture, the Fathers of the Church and in particular Saint Thomas Aquinas.

Giovanni Battista Tornatore was particularly well versed in philosophy: his mind was quick and inclined to speculation and metaphysics.

Later he would address in articles and publications many questions concerning the problem of knowledge and other philosophical discussions. No less would be his interest in dogmatic and moral theology.

The places of study were quite lively and were beginning to feel the effects of the debates and issues raised by rationalism, the Enlightenment, Jansenism and later Rosmini’s proposals. There was great ferment, then, together with constant appeals to remain faithful to orthodoxy, to the Church and to her Magisterium. Yet all this took place in a spirit of freedom and of working out deep convictions. With full respect for this freedom, G.B. Tornatore gradually increased his store of learning and stood out for his diligence, his constant application and the synthesis he was already beginning to develop.

Presented by his Superiors to the Vicariate of Rome for approval of his suitability for the priesthood and for authorization to hear confessions, Tornatore was ordained a priest on 15 March 1844.

Immediately afterward he was given the task of teaching mathematics, philosophy and theology to the missionary students in Rome; he was already able to pass on learning and his own spiritual experience in a mature way. While still young he had come into contact and friendship with Blessed Gaspare del Bufalo and Vincenzo Pallotti, and he also knew and greatly admired Bernardo Maria Clausi, whom he would later always call my angel. Tornatore combined doctrine and learning with piety and holiness of life, and with a spirit of benevolence and Christian charity.

A lover of assiduous prayer, he devoted much time to adoration of the Eucharistic sacrament and celebrated Holy Mass with devotion and recollection. Formed in the school of Saint Vincent, he also favored the works of Saint John of the Cross, Father Scaramelli’s Mystical Directory and the theological works of Suárez. Endowed with higher lights, he devoted himself selflessly to hearing confessions and directing the souls who came in great numbers to ask for advice and to find serenity and peace. “He had,” notes a disciple, “an open and steady gaze and an almost smiling mouth; just looking at him inspired trust.”3 “For direction and advice not only church people but also lay people turned to him, and they went away fully satisfied. They called him father, although that title is not used among the sons of Saint Vincent...”4

He led a simple and rather poor life. He gave everyone proof of very great humility and obedience. Committed to ascetic effort, he shaped his life according to the teachings of the Imitation of Christ.

His personality, both culturally and spiritually, showed remarkable depth, so much so that he was soon singled out and in some way prepared to take on teaching and research posts in a more suitable and qualified setting, as would shortly be the case at the Alberoni College in Piacenza.

In 1852 he was in fact sent to the College of San Lazzaro to hold the chair of Sacred Scripture, with the task of director of the young students of the Mission. Later he was appointed to the chairs of Dogmatic and Moral Theology, and he would teach at this prestigious college for almost 25 years.

But what was the Alberoni and what did it stand for?

f. The Alberoni College

The College of San Lazzaro, founded by Cardinal Alberoni (who gave it his name) in 1733, was at once entrusted to the Priests of the Congregation of the Mission, established precisely for the education and formation of churchmen as well as for the holy missions.5 Why this union between Vincent and Cardinal Alberoni? Boiardi sees in it a dialectic and mutual complementarity between diplomacy and simplicity, power and service, the man of war and the one who gathers up the victims of war, the minister of a great Prince for whom he wishes to prepare a dominion and the minister of Christ who seeks only to extend his Kingdom in souls and in the world. Both, however, were united by the plan of working to form good and zealous priests.

Cardinal G. Alberoni had come to know the Vincentian Missionaries of the House of Montecitorio at first hand, a short distance from his first Roman residence; he had seen the enthusiasm aroused around the figure of their founder Vincent de Paul, beatified in 1729; and for nearly a century the whole clergy of Rome had gone to the House of the Mission as to their own home. So he was convinced that the Priests of the Mission, who had suggested to him the foundation of the College of San Lazzaro, were the priests closest to his ideal and the best suited to direct his College. With his Missionaries, Saint Vincent de Paul thus entered Cardinal Alberoni’s College.

The history of the College was now traced out for ever, for centuries: the Cardinal and Saint Vincent would be its architects; the one would bring all the elements that would give it life, the other his method and technique of priestly formation. Without this mutual contribution the College would not be what it is. Without Saint Vincent the College would have been something else, just as it would have been something else without the Cardinal’s foundation, legislation and organization.6

Equipped from the start with suitable resources - libraries rich in old collections and fully up to date in philosophical, theological, literary and historical works, physics and natural science laboratories - the Alberoni College offered ample opportunities for study, inquiry and research.

Its highly qualified teaching staff carried on from the beginning a brilliant tradition, scientifically and culturally praiseworthy.

Also noteworthy is the sentire cum Ecclesia (= communion with the Church), which gave flavor to studies and made them mature into authentic programs of spirituality, keeping them from the temptation of party schools and their often sterile and negative disputes.

“It is clear that in an atmosphere of such warm prestige for learning, and in the climate of a centuries-old Tradition now so vibrant with approval and goodwill, both teachers and students would feel almost unconsciously drawn to derive every possible benefit from it and committed to keeping its flame ever more alive and high.

But I want to say something even more beautiful and interesting: I want to reveal to you the soul of this Tradition, a soul which, linking it with the Vincentian spirit and method of education, makes it a truly vital instrument of ecclesiastical formation. For the Missionaries, while devoting themselves earnestly and seriously to study and teaching, have always taken care, following Saint Vincent’s directives, to teach nothing but the doctrine of the Church. Just as in spiritual formation they do not claim to have a school of “spirituality” of their own, so in the intellectual formation of the clergy they neither have nor want a “school” of their own, nor do they take sides with any. They have always set out the traditional doctrine of the Church and have not entered the fray of controversial questions. They confine themselves to presenting the content and the respective positions; they have never sided with any particular “School”. They have always followed Saint Thomas, obeying the Church in this too; and they have done so wonderfully, dedicating the «Divus Thomas» to the Saint and his thought.”7

g. A professor in suspicious times

The College remained orthodox and consequently always rejected the charge of Jansenism. The priests of the Mission, Fr. Tornatore included, would unfortunately be the target of accusers and even be denounced to the Holy See. But these were in reality slanderous maneuvers, as Prof. Aristide Bosoni would later show.8

The charge of Jansenism originated with Donnino Copellotti on the occasion of the Alberoni academic disputations of 1762 on the De praedestinatione Sanctorum (= the predestination of the saints), and gave rise to a controversy between Copellotti (backed by the Molinists) and the Augustinians, who were joined by the Friars Minor and others of the secular clergy of Piacenza. The Priests of the Mission teaching at San Lazzaro officially stayed out of the controversy, even though in practice they (especially Francesco Grassi, author of the disputed set of academic theses) were the main target of the Molinist accusers.

With the passing of the years that regrettable controversy gradually faded into the background, but without dying out. The fact that the Alberoni disputations of 1762 had also been reported in the «Nouvelles Ecclésiastiques» could be exploited as confirmation that the charge was supposedly true. Twice in fact (in 1793 and 1850), almost as an echo of those accusations, the masters of San Lazzaro were even denounced to the Holy See as Jansenists by the Ducal Court of Parma; on another occasion, in 1802, the accusation stopped at Parma. But all three times the accusations, which in reality were not aimed at safeguarding Catholic doctrine, proved to be slanderous maneuvers. The memory of those inquiries remained, however, and superficial scholars took no account of the innocence established by the investigations; indeed, without examining the documents, they assumed those accusations were true. “Slander, slander... something always sticks.” And sadly that is what happened. Such scholars, careless and ill-informed, erected elaborate constructions and presented them as true history, when they were merely the fruit of their imagination. A typical example is Ettore Rota, who, writing on Pietro Tamburini in 1912 and later on Giuseppe Poggi in 1923, went so far as to describe the Alberoni teaching as a march “toward Calvinism” and the theses of 1762 as “the Jansenist thunderbolt” that burst within the walls of the Alberoni College like a new “Wittenberg protest”.

This denigrating procedure, which preliminary archival soundings revealed to rest on a non-existent reality, prompted the extensive, deep and careful research of Dr. Don Aristide Bosoni. His 1926 dissertation brought to light how slanderous the Jansenist accusations against the Alberoni College really were, and his work, merely noted by the «Bollettino Storico Piacentino», drew to Piacenza scholars of Jansenism, some from France, who confirmed Dr. Bosoni’s conclusions; in Italy, however, it was ignored by latecomers such as Catalano, who in 1950 tagged along behind the long-buried Rota, letting himself be carried by him.9

The Alberoni College looked to Saint Thomas10 as an exemplary master of philosophy and theology and, without intending to be innovative, nevertheless opened itself to the debate then under way and contributed to it scientifically, publishing from 1879 (the first issue would appear in 1880) the prestigious review «Divus Thomas».11 It would be in contact with Louvain, France, Germany and Rome.

It should be noted that a few months later (4 August 1879) Leo XIII’s encyclical Aeterni Patris would be published.

The review Divus Thomas, conceived and organized by a man such as Alberto Barberis12 with the active collaboration of Tornatore13 and Professors C. Ramellini and G.B. Vinati, aimed to be an aid14 for academies and schools devoted to Scholasticism.

“The «Program», signed «Directores», sets out what this aid will consist of:

1. - An exposition of Aquinas’s doctrine, made directly from his works. - This exposition must exclude not only all pretense but every bias; instead, by applying the rules of sound criticism, it must bring to light: a) the genuine thought of Saint Thomas: «quaenam fuerit Sapientis intentio»; b) the ways he followed to set it out; c) the contribution thus made to scientific and religious progress. - An objective exposition of Saint Thomas’s thought, therefore, conducted with scientific and critical criteria. But, lest it be supposed that the aim was to promote a movement of pure Thomism, ignoring the countless excellent Thomistic studies of the past and of recent times, the «Program» goes on to give the assurance that the Review will also undertake:

2. - To make known and appreciate the old and recent studies on Saint Thomas, both those that sought only to comment and those that also developed Thomist doctrines. Indeed, room will be found in the Review even for those who most distinguished themselves in the struggle against the Angelic Doctor. We are thus far removed from narrow fetishism or narrowness of ideas.

3. - Finally, to offer more immediate help to the Academies, the Review proposes to study in depth the philosophical traditions of those that call themselves Thomist, and to provide information on the contemporary Thomist movement in Schools and Academies, both ecclesiastical and lay.

Among the practical benefits the Review hopes to bring, the «Program» mentions two in particular: 1) to contribute to the increase and strengthening of scientific institutes devoted to the study of Saint Thomas’s doctrine; 2) to allow seminarians to find in the Review the equivalent of the chair of Thomism that cannot be established in most ecclesiastical institutes.

It is above all this last detail that reveals to us the deeply Vincentian soul of the one who hid behind the anonymous «Directores» while being in fact its real founder and moving spirit: Mr. Alberto Barberis, C.M. The Review would certainly speak to the learned and to scholars, but it would also address seminarians in order to contribute positively to their formation, a contribution that was to consist not in a greater or lesser mass of notions, nor in an increase of culture, but in giving young seminarians a suitable means of developing in them the capacity to penetrate the depths of the sacred sciences and to contemplate them: «ad sacras scientias introspiciendas et mentes ad contemplationem exercendas».

“When in 1852 the Lazarists returned to the College from the Roman province, they favored an open Thomism, that is, one that was not a repetitive formalism. Among the newcomers was Fr. Giovanni Battista Tornatore, who together with Carlo Ramellini and Alberto Barberis would launch the review Divus Thomas, a training ground for Thomism, yet open also to the critical findings of biblical science and to dialogue with modern culture.”15

In his Brief of 9 October 1882 Leo XIII praised the priests of Piacenza who “undertook to expound and spread the doctrine of Saint Thomas” through Divus Thomas.

«La Civiltà Cattolica» also highlighted the papal document and on 23 December 1882, “reviewing the book by G.B. Tornatore of Piacenza, Expositio principii traditi ad naturam investigandam rei substantialis (Piacenza 1882), the reviewer, certainly Fr. Cornoldi, admitted: ‘As regards knowing, he stands with Aquinas.’ As regards being, ‘it would have been better if Tornatore had expressed his idea more clearly; nevertheless he can be defended against the charge of falling into the Rosminian theory.’ Although using a terminology different from that of Saint Thomas, his doctrine is ‘opposed to the Rosminian system, and we hope that it will always show itself so’; and he hoped that the review «Divus Thomas», praised in Leo XIII’s ‘most beautiful letter’ to the Bishop of Piacenza, would fully and clearly uphold the main points of Aquinas’s doctrine (Rivista della stampa italiana, La Civiltà Cattolica, v. I, series XII, pp. 72-83).”16

The Bishop of Piacenza, G.B. Scalabrini (1839-1905), encouraged the initiative since it fitted into his plan to rebuild the cultural and spiritual fabric of his clergy, “but in a spirit that was not intransigent, based not on a rejection of modern culture, but on a line of reconciliation between the Church and the world.”17

The Alberoni, like the culturally liveliest seminaries, was in the years 1835-1860 rather attentive to new ideas and often attracted by Rosmini’s philosophy too. It is true that through Buroni18 the Alberoni clarified its openness and specified the criteria of cultural formation and the doctrine dictated by orthodoxy, but the accusations were not spared for all that.

The condemnation of Rosmini’s works Delle cinque piaghe and La Costituzione secondo la giustizia sociale had in fact accelerated in Rome a regressive process that would strike hard. And so the Alberoni too would be caught in the storm.

The charges were Jansenism, Gallicanism, Giobertism, Rosminianism and liberalism.

The missionaries then presented to the Superior General, J.B. Étienne, who had come to Piacenza from Paris expressly, a long memorandum, owed at least in large part to Buroni’s pen, as the draft I found in Turin proves. Fr. Étienne’s intervention helped to prove the groundlessness of the specific doctrinal accusations, but not to untangle completely the skein of suspicions, misunderstandings and fears. In some sectors of the clergy there was a mood hostile to the College, linked to a view that was too static and undifferentiated. Buroni commented: “Just as in Galileo’s day people were afraid to put their eye to the telescope for fear of losing the faith, so they shrink all the more from any return and progress of civilization etc. etc., and at the beginning of the Pontificate of Pius IX they viewed his acts with suspicion and judged them with suspicion. Given all this, it is no wonder that they take us for liberals and heretics, and our students with us.” Those responsible for this attitude were not so much the gestures as the intransigent part of the clergy of Piacenza, which saw in probabilism, Molinism and conservative Aristotelianism a bulwark against the spread of revolution, Jansenism and liberalism. Bishop Ranza too shared this mentality, an “old-fashioned bishop” who, though possessed of solid culture, was inclined to intransigence.19

But the Alberoni and its review Divus Thomas were in no way pro-Rosminian; the Alberoni line was not that of “a generic concordism between Rosmini and Saint Thomas”, even though the Civiltà Cattolica, reviewing Tornatore’s works, repeatedly insisted on it, pointing out “the danger involved in abandoning traditional Scholastic terminology”.20

Particularly heated would be the controversy in defense of Tornatore, sparked by the attacks of G. Ballerini and M. Autore. Ballerini accused the Alberoni professor of being a Rosminian. Tornatore clarified his position by reaffirming his basic profession and distancing himself from Rosmini.21 Barberis too, as a faithful disciple of Tornatore, felt he should speak out in his favor and set out in the review Divus Thomas his assessments, which completely cleared his professor.22

h. Between lecture hall and church

Through his teaching, research and publications Tornatore was at the center of the academic life of the Alberoni, entered into dialogue with the Italian and European culture of the time and made a significant contribution. From the second half of the nineteenth century the spiritual climate took its cue from the acts of Pius IX, such as the Syllabus, the definition of the Immaculate Conception and the universal jurisdiction and infallibility of the Pope, and sought to bring the Church back into the ferment of ideas and movements. Tornatore’s activity was on this same wavelength. On the one hand he wanted to fight the new and pernicious ideas of modernism and defend the Church from them; on the other he was committed to encouraging and promoting study, but along the lines of orthodoxy.

The Church’s doctrine clashed with the ideas advocated by modernism. This term denotes “a movement of ideas among Catholic scholars which, between the end of the nineteenth and the beginning of the twentieth century, advocated a substantial reform of the traditional conceptions of dogma and of Christian life, while not destroying their forms of expression and structures, committing the Church to adapt to even the most radical principles of modern philosophies. With modernism one arrives at radical and universal statements of principle, inasmuch as theological science is led to subordinate itself to philosophical premises taken wholesale from modern thought, and the Church to let itself be transformed by the world rather than to transform it. Not a partial selection of the fragments of truth in modern errors, but a total abdication of traditional truths before modern ‘truths’.”23

On the advice and at the express wish of the Bishop of Piacenza, Msgr. Ranza, Tornatore published a volume, Commento dell'Angelico Dottore S. Tommaso d'Aquino de' Predicatori, alle decretali d'Innocenzo III, in which he illustrated with accuracy and precision, as well as fine subtlety, Aquinas’s teaching on the mystery of the Most Holy Trinity.24

He had also planned a similar study on the mystery of the Incarnation, which however he was unable to complete because he was meanwhile taken up with other activities.25

His adoption of the textbooks by Charles-René Billuart and Giovanni Perrone is emblematic in this respect. He showed a deep knowledge of the theological disciplines, and to students who were rather amazed at his mastery of the subject he would reply kindly: “Study hard, and in the author you will find what I find there.”

“What his teaching lacked,” writes Tononi, “was the support of auxiliary disciplines such as philology, history, archaeology, biblical and modern exegesis and the like...”26 Nevertheless there is unanimous agreement in recognizing Tornatore as “a most learned and erudite man, wise and expert in knowledge”. Authoritative voices and well-known writers observed in the Revue Thomiste that Tornatore deserves praise for his profound doctrine drawn from lofty and pure sources.27

The times were indeed not easy: suspicion, accusation and not infrequently slander spread easily.

In spite of all this, however, Tornatore was a passionate seeker of truth and knowledge. His scholarly record is therefore highly positive.

But Tornatore was not only lecture hall and library, since he was above all church and pulpit: the celebration of the Eucharist and constant adoration of it, preaching the word of God through missions, and spiritual direction. From 1852 to 1895 Father Tornatore generously rendered a precious service to the ever-growing number of people who came to him for light and to resolve their doubts, to make progress on the path of goodness and charity. Rome too asked his opinion on questions of metaphysics. Colleagues, students, religious and lay people all had in him a point of reference.

From 1866 onwards, as the work God had entrusted to Rosa Gattorno began to develop in Piacenza, he devoted himself to it tirelessly, offering her his help and collaboration. At first he took an interest and followed its course from outside; then little by little he opened himself more and more to the work, which he hoped would be called the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne, as indeed it was, because the Lord had directly inspired the Foundress that this was to be its name.28

Fully involved in guiding the Institute, Fr. Tornatore wrote the Rules, in which he set down the key elements of its spirituality; he provided for many temporal needs of the new foundation, followed its progress and development with interest and love, and rejoiced that the seed planted in the garden was growing and bearing fruits of charity for the life of the world.

The Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne thus became for Tornatore the apple of his eye, the life of his life, the chief commitment of his existence.

He would shoulder enormous labors, face delicate and complex tasks, and establish contacts and relations with well-known figures in order to help, protect and defend the Institute.

He consequently widened the scope of his charity, and when he left his chair at the Alberoni in 1877 he became a pilgrim like Saint Vincent and directed other institutes, such as that of the Handmaids of the Sanctuary.

Sober and a lover of the ascetic life, he resolved in God and through faith in him the trials and humiliations he underwent. In this way he cultivated the virtues of humility, meekness and charity, and built his life upon them. For this reason he would commonly be called Fr. Tornatore the saint, the friend of the saints, the father of many unfortunates, and at the same time the friend of many gentlemen.

In 1888, “having withdrawn from the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne to the house of Montecitorio” in Rome, he continued to teach mathematics to the students and to render other useful spiritual services to his confreres. In 1890 he returned once again to the Alberoni College and lent a hand at the Institute for the poor suffering from scrofula, remaining available to them for a good four years.

He was zealous in preaching and evangelizing.

On 26 July 1891 the statue of Our Lady of Santa Maria del Taro was crowned. Father Tornatore, together with Father Baratelli, had preached the preparatory mission.

i. The birth of an idea

1. From a chance meeting, the idea of a project

Anyone who has been fortunate enough to meet a great personality knows from experience that they have received a truly indelible impression, message or sign!

While still a novice, Tornatore met in Rome a priest and religious of the Congregation of Saint Francis of Paola, a certain Fr. Bernardo Clausi.

But who was he? Why was he already rather famous? And why do people still speak of him, both among the Minims and in the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne and in the Congregations?

Vincenzo Maria, born at San Sisto dei Valdesi (Cosenza) on 24 November 1789, was baptized the following day in his parish.

In 1805 he entered the first friary of the Minims at the Sanctuary of Paola.

After completing the canonical year of novitiate he could not consecrate himself to the Lord because he had not reached the required age. He therefore had to wait; meanwhile he was called up and had to serve his country. In 1818 he was ordained a priest and carried out his ministry with great dignity and zeal. In 1827 he began a second novitiate with the Minims and was at last able to make his vows of religious profession and receive his new name, Bernardo Maria.

Religious life and priesthood would be the track of his existence, whether at the Sanctuary of Paola or in Rome at the College of the Minims. Meanwhile his fame spread; he was pointed out and became the object of much attention. For this reason his superiors, in agreement with the authorities of the Vicariate, thought it best to send him elsewhere. And so Fr. Bernardo, like Saint Francis of Paola, became a wayfarer of God on the roads of men. Paola, Rome, Naples, Cosenza, some cities of Piedmont and many cities of Italy were the places of his witness of faith and Gospel service. Fr. Clausi made the charism of his Founder shine forth and became a clear and highly qualified sign of it. During the cholera of 1837, like Cardinal Federico Borromeo and the Capuchin Fathers in Milan, like Cardinal Dusmet in Catania, he overcame every barrier and difficulty to help the afflicted, relieve their suffering and prepare everyone for the meeting with the Father. Everyone acknowledged in him very special mystical gifts, accompanied by extraordinary phenomena.

For many years of his life he would be subjected to trials, anguish of spirit and terrible afflictions, but he constantly responded by accepting God’s will and professing his faith in private and in public: I believe, he would say, I firmly believe!

He had a special devotion to and veneration for the Blessed Virgin Mary and her Mother Saint Anne. Many remember above all his convincing arguments and this vibrant experience of his, which shone through every pore and could win every heart. But let us look at his first meeting with Fr. Tornatore and some of its consequences.

Their first meeting was by chance, in the street, when his companions pointed him out as the Saint everyone in Rome was talking about. Tornatore thought to himself: “If you are a saint, pray for me.” At once Fr. Bernardo turned to look at him with a gracious smile. Tornatore was then so edified by Clausi’s outstanding virtues that he would call him “my Angel”; after Clausi’s death he collaborated actively with the Postulator of his Cause of beatification, Fr. Agostino Donadio, gathering recollections and spreading his image, and particularly in writing the first biography of Clausi, published in 1885 under Donadio’s name. Together with him, while at the Alberoni College in Piacenza, he also worked closely with the Servant of God Rosa Gattorno on the foundation of the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne, an Institute foretold by Clausi and visibly protected from its origins by his heavenly patronage.29 On Clausi’s prophecy concerning this Institute, here is what Tornatore himself wrote to a religious Daughter of Saint Anne: “The Venerable Fr. Bernardo M. Clausi is the one the Lord used to found the Institute (...). At the beginning, when the Mother came to Piacenza to found an Institute, she came with some Daughters who were called Daughters of Mary Immaculate (...). I told her of my devotion to my Angel, Father Bernardo, and told her that my Servant of God had for many years inspired me30 to found an Institute of Daughters of Saint Anne, and so, if she wanted to be directed by me, it would be good for the Daughters to be called Daughters of Saint Anne, Mother of Mary Immaculate, instead of Daughters of Mary. To make known to the Mother that this was his will, the Lord caused the holy Mother Saint Anne and his faithful Servant, the Venerable Fr. Bernardo, to appear to the Mother and make known to her that it was pleasing to God that the Institute should be the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne. You see, then, my daughter, how true it is that the Daughters of Saint Anne ought to be very devoted to the Venerable Fr. Bernardo, my angel? Oh, how many graces they would receive if they prayed to him!”31

Fr. Bernardo Maria Clausi’s presence would be strong: during his lifetime for Fr. Tornatore, and mystically for Mother Rosa. The Lazarist Father stresses that Fr. Bernardo was his angel, while Mother Gattorno speaks of a continuous and fruitful dialogue from which she received light and comfort, guidance and enlightenment. In other words, we can rightly say that Fr. Bernardo had a considerable influence on the shaping of the project of the Daughters of Saint Anne and on the journey of the Institute. It is in this light that the decision of the General Chapter of the Minims to associate the Daughters of Saint Anne with the Order should be seen.

Fr. Bernardo Clausi died on 20 December 1849, mourned by the people who had loved him and by his confreres, who had been constantly edified by his life and witness.

It seems only right to give in its essential lines a message that Fr. A. Bellantonio reproduces at the end of his work on Clausi.

“Bernardo Clausi was neither a writer nor an orator, although he fully carried out the duties of the sacred ministry. In him an outstanding Gospel witness shone forth in his concrete daily conduct. His message lies chiefly in this. He preached, he cried out with his life, as has been said; he wrote in the letters of duty the faithful fulfilment of the Word of God that saves us.

The commandments and precepts, the virtues and the spirit of the beatitudes (the latter as practical criteria and a way of life suited to making the former easier to keep), piety and living participation in the liturgy and the sacraments were the setting of his eloquent message of consistency and fidelity, as well as of fervor and perfection.

Father Bernardo showed toward God an outstanding human and Christian consistency and a fervent fidelity to his will, in keeping with the totality proper to the greatest of the commandments: with all one’s heart, all one’s soul, all one’s strength. He responded to Christ with sincere and unconditional supernatural adherence and with obedience to his Gospel. He lived in communion with all the members of the Church, beginning with the sacred Pastors, accepting their teaching and discipline. Moreover, he daily professed the rule of life he had embraced through vows in the religious Family of the Minims, and followed it by vocation, in the spirit of the Founder from Paola, as a specific and sure path to holiness.

For all these reasons Clausi is a thoroughly reliable witness of Christian, religious and priestly life, having experienced in his own person what he also taught on these matters as a minister of God and pointed out with the inspiration of a guide and counselor in the ways of the spirit. His message is therefore sure and convincing, and it reaches beyond his contemporaries into a continuous present, because of the Gospel source in which it is rooted and the authenticity of its transmission.

There is, however, a series of personal experiences of the spirit and of asceticism, of trials and, in general, of inner and outward conduct, in which this message is given by Clausi’s response to the initiative of Grace, or to God’s action upon him, whether by his will, his permission or his good pleasure. This is the other pole of the exemplary character that gives strength and content to Father Bernardo’s message. Through it he is not only a witness but always a living point of reference for edification and conduct: a sign of how Grace leads and of how the man of God responds.

The message of this witness, favored by supernatural attraction, and of this living sign, tested by the alternation of light and darkness and by deepening tribulation, is indeed manifold and valid; to listen to it is to reflect on his moral and spiritual example in ordinary and extraordinary circumstances, on the way of asceticism and purifying trial, in the successive ascents of the spirit, including the most acute trial.

“This is the way, this is the trial in which God wants me,” Father Bernardo would say, adding: “Who has ever known the ways of God? Who has ever been his counselor?” and “This is a mystery... Let God act.”

The path along which God led him in the crucial period of his greatest trial was among the hardest, and follows the way described by the Mystical Doctor. For a fidelity tested to the utmost, and therefore more meritorious, the desert of spiritual dryness opened up before him. He had to cross it by the light of pure faith, in the dark night, in which he experienced loneliness and abandonment. He felt as if rejected and cast off; yet he did not give in to terror and despair.

Though terribly tried and afflicted by desolation, he remained constantly hand in hand with God, even in the dark, calling upon him with unutterable groanings, longing for him alone with all the strength of his spirit, sure that he would see the light again in him who hears the cry of the poor. At times God himself inspired him with this certainty, making him a prophet.

After such a trial, Clausi’s example and words have greater force, and his message greater credibility.”32

2. The originality of a name

At a superficial glance no one distinguishes between one person and another, one religious and another! Looking more closely, however, we notice differences and characteristics, nuances and basic orientations. We then realize that each person is different from the other, and that every institute and congregation has had its own particular tone from its very name. Yes indeed! The name is truly important and at once gives the basic perspective and in some way the constitutive reality.

To it, in fact, the charism and spirituality, the style and all that will in time make up the heritage of the Institute itself will then be linked.

Seen in this light, the Founders’ effort of insight is quite clear, together with their commitment to bring a new reality to life by reading events with the eyes of faith, scrutinizing the signs of the times and illuminating them with the light of the Gospel. This is the history of the Church, the history of spirituality, the history of all the orders, religious institutes and congregations. It is a common denominator and a splendid human and divine reality in which the Spirit and the holy people of God are at work, embracing the human family.

The Vincentian Father, as already mentioned, had long cherished the idea of the birth of a congregation inspired by Saint Anne, Mother of Mary Immaculate, and named after her. Fr. Giovanni Battista Tornatore, having begun to glimpse in Mother Rosa the one who was bringing to life the Institute foretold by Fr. Bernardo Maria Clausi, began to tell her of his friendship with him and of the devotion Clausi had fostered toward Saint Anne, Mother of Mary Immaculate. He also mentioned a dream of his: “I would be curious to know whether the Nuns I saw in a dream years ago, in the month of glorious Saint Anne (I believe the dream was truly divine), were some of yours.”33

Mother Rosa, for her part, states: “As soon as I arrived in this hovel (the contract was signed on 26 March 1866, so the event must be placed before the letter Fr. Tornatore wrote to Mother Rosa on 4 July 1866), I looked for a little room in not too bad a state to make into the small chapel, which the Bishop blessed, and he left the Lord there. Oh, how happy I felt to have my Beloved with me, and I spent whole nights there. Ah, what did I not receive! One evening, while I was alone and praying intensely, and in my very prayer felt such intimate union with God, the little Chapel was lit up by a great light, and the Most Holy Virgin and Saint Anne appeared, and lower down, as if kneeling before the Most Holy Virgin, Saint Francis of Assisi. The Immaculate said distinctly and in a clear voice: I wish the title of the rules to be Daughters of Saint Anne, my Mother (and here she pointed her out to me). I give this work to my Mother with great satisfaction; do not be distressed, I will always consider whatever you do for her as done to me.”34

It was therefore only after the intervention of Mary Immaculate that Mother Rosa was led to accept the name “Daughters of Saint Anne” for the Institute.

As regards Saint Anne, it is worth recalling that in the years 1855-1865 reflection on the cult of Mary Immaculate and on devotion to her Mother Saint Anne had gone through a particularly fruitful and deep period.

Fr. Cremisini,35 a priest of the Mission, by publishing an essay on Saint Anne as early as 1862, had offered an interesting reflection from both a theological and a devotional point of view.

Having placed Saint Anne within the mystery of Salvation, the Author focuses on her specific role in relation to Mary Immaculate and consequently to the Incarnate Word. Hence the cult of Saint Anne as an expression of a typical devotion to the Immaculate.

Starting from God’s Plan, Cremisini stresses Anne’s role: in her womb is formed the Ark of the New Covenant, that is Mary; in her womb the new heavens and the new earth are formed. In that temple “there was the Father to sanctify his Daughter, the Word to enrich his Mother with every heavenly delight, the Holy Spirit to adorn his Bride with every grace.”36 Devotion to Saint Anne therefore leads to devotion to the Most Holy Virgin Immaculate, her most worthy Daughter.

Clothed in humility and modesty, Saint Anne is a model of openness to God, who does great things in her and with her. Saint Anne is the mother of the one who, like the morning star, was to come to gladden the world and, like the dawn, was to bring it the eternal sun of justice, Jesus Christ, Savior and Redeemer.

Gifted with contemplation and activity, Saint Anne has a deep understanding of the divine Scriptures; rich in the virtues of faith, hope and charity, Saint Anne walks the paths of justice and takes her place on the road already traveled by the Patriarchs and Prophets.

Saint Anne and her husband Joachim were chosen to be the grandparents of Christ our Lord, and so the parents of his Most Holy Mother.

We should therefore note, on the one hand, Saint Anne’s close connection with the mystery of salvation, above all with the Persons of the Holy Trinity and with Mary, Immaculate Virgin and Mother of the Savior, and on the other the consequent and natural devotion of the Christian people.

At this point we ask: what is the role and function of Saint Anne for Fr. Tornatore? What shape do the cult and devotion of the “Daughters of Saint Anne” take?

There is no doubt that Father Tornatore knew the publication of his confrere Fr. Cremisini and that he was also inspired by it.

In the light of his most significant writings, the Rules and Letters, his thought is clear. He sees in the person of Saint Anne a role of capital importance and at the same time a true model of life. Saint Anne cooperates in the plan of salvation in a special way by bringing into the world Mary Most Holy, who is Immaculate, and by committing herself to a simple, hidden life full of virtue.

On the basis of this theological knowledge and other interesting insights, Fr. Tornatore was glad to work with Mother Rosa on drawing up the constitutions.

In the long run the name would have to develop the spirituality and so grow into a charismatic reality, that great whole which structures the life of religious at the level of their constitution and foundation, yet which in fact will always be rather hard to explain. For a charism is not so much something to be discussed as always a very particular way of life that reveals a mystery of Christ.

It is precisely to life that Fr. Tornatore refers in a letter intended to make the Institute known:

“The specific purpose that distinguishes the Daughters of Saint Anne... is to make profession of giving special veneration to glorious Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate.

Its aim is to give veneration and honor to the august Mother of the Immaculate, glorious Saint Anne, precisely because she is Mother of the Immaculate: a truly singular veneration and honor, such as poor creatures can give her.

This then is our profession: so that if one of us is asked, ‘Why has God called you to this Institute?’, she replies: ‘To know, love and honor with a wholly singular honor, such as she receives from no other Institute in the Church, glorious Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate, precisely under this title of Mother of the Immaculate; and this, of course, to please God, Jesus her Grandson, and Mary Immaculate her daughter.’

That is why we bear the name of daughters of Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate.

To attain this aim: 1. We try to imitate her virtues as recorded in our Rules: we make the four annual vows of Poverty, Chastity, Obedience and Assistance to the sick.

2. We imitate her Religion toward Jesus by perpetual adoration in his Sacrament of love; her compassion toward Jesus sick in the sick; and her devotion to the Child Jesus, by caring for poor young girls in danger.”37

On many other occasions he returned to the subject to explain simply the character of the Institute and what was specific to it.

“The aim that the daughters of Saint Anne share with all Christians is to please God by faith, hope and charity and by the practice of good works; the specific aim that distinguishes them from any other religious body is to make profession of giving a wholly particular veneration to glorious Saint Anne under the title of Mother of the Immaculate. They are thus distinguished from ordinary devotees of the Saint, because these incur no obligation to have special devotion to her; the daughters of Saint Anne, on the contrary, profess a distinctive honor to her. And if some Christian made a vow of singular love for Saint Anne, the daughter of Saint Anne would still be distinguished, because she belongs to a body consecrated to a singular love for the Saint, whereas he is a mere private individual. So if a daughter of Saint Anne is asked, ‘What does God want of you?’, she replies: ‘He wants and commands me in my vocation to give a wholly special veneration to glorious Saint Anne.’ So my ultimate end is to please God, Jesus Christ and Mary Most Holy, and the proximate end of my vocation is to please glorious Saint Anne in order to please God.”38

In this Fr. Tornatore follows the sacramental approach found, with different tones and nuances, in many orders and congregations. In the monastic world, for example, the Abbot is the one who takes the place of Christ, while for the Benedictine Sisters of the Blessed Sacrament the first Superior of the house is Our Lady.

The insistence on regarding Saint Anne as the superior of the Institute, and then of the various houses, is meant to emphasize on the one hand the dimension of faith, an essential condition of all religious life, and on the other to bring out the Institute’s own charism, closely linked to the Mother of Mary Immaculate.

Nor should we overlook the catechetical method he used to impress and engrave more deeply on the mind the basic content of this teaching.

Through daily insistence and the corresponding practice, the whole of life would be shaped and would acquire the new spiritual mentality.

“Among the other virtues, the Institute also professes the compassion of Saint Anne’s heart, by assisting the sick in their homes... In the same way they take in poor girls in danger to keep them from losing their innocence and virtue: and here too they honor the care that (Saint Anne) took of the Immaculate Child and the zeal which, through this care, the Saint must have had to see all the young girls in the world innocent.”

The title Daughters of Saint Anne therefore expresses worship and life, devotion and practice, relationship with the Mother of Mary Immaculate and relationship with one’s brothers and sisters.

It is a name that must penetrate the depths of each religious’s conscience until invocation of the Saint, and so devotion to her, as well as imitation of her in various circumstances and in apostolic activities, become natural and indispensable. Saint Anne must therefore be support, guide and even a shining star; and to know how to live by her, Mary is pointed out as the model fully realized in herself.39

For this reason Fr. Tornatore, wishing to win over the sisters, would point to Saint Anne as the first superior of the Institute, “She rules it, defends it, governs it”,40 and together with Mother Rosa would insistently ask that she be continually invoked by all the communities.

The aspiration “Blessed be our glorious Mother Saint Anne, Mother of Mary Immaculate”, like the prayer of the Russian Pilgrim, was to become life and to be a continual profession of faith.

“This aspiration contains a profession of faith, by which we believe that Mary, in the womb of our holy Mother, was conceived Immaculate in the first instant of her conception... And since this aspiration is almost continuous from morning to evening, by means of it the Institute makes as it were a continual act of faith in the immaculate conception of Mary.”41

Veneration of Saint Anne is therefore not the end point of true piety, since it must lead to Mary and to her Son Jesus; moreover, it must never turn into sterile devotionalism.

The Circular Letter of 1880 speaks of the recognition granted by Leo XIII, highlights the most noble name of daughters of Saint Anne and gives news of the spread of the Institute.

“See, dearest Sisters and daughters, our Institute, the family of the august and glorious Saint Anne, Mother of Mary Immaculate and our Mother, has entered the fourteenth year of its existence: a year which we hope will bring it much glory, as did the year just ended.

Yes, sisters, very many were the divine mercies with which the year ’79 was filled. The greatest, the most deeply felt and splendid, is that Holy Church, through her currently reigning Vicar Leo XIII, has definitively recognized our family as a Religious family, which is to say as a family of God; it therefore has that approval which allows not the slightest doubt that those who gather in it find there all the means to reach that distinguished holiness to which God calls those who make special profession of the evangelical counsels of Poverty, Chastity and Obedience. As a result, the goodwill of people toward us, who bear the most noble name of daughters of Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate, is seen to grow ever greater, since they are sure that this name, the most honorable for a creature, was not taken by us but imposed on us by Heaven. A clear testimony of this goodwill is the many requests we have received to found houses in various places.”42

The Institute deserves credit for having contributed greatly to spreading the cult of Saint Anne and for having read the charism in a biblical perspective, highlighting the role of Anne and Joachim and linking it with that of the anawim who awaited the Lord.

The charism has gained enormously from this: its basic orientation has been consolidated and the momentum given to it has been set on a path of broadening and maturing. One might perhaps compare this process to the effort that for centuries characterized the ecclesial community when it sought to grasp the richness of the senses of Holy Scripture.

By then linking the originality of the charism, in its essentials, to the theological, liturgical, ecclesial and spiritual development of the Council and of the contemporary world, the Institute has set out some significant orientations more in keeping with the mystery of Christ, more in line with the application of the Gospel and more relevant to modern life.

l. Towards the Father

Towards the end of 1894, ill with pulmonary tuberculosis, Fr. Tornatore was lovingly cared for by his confreres. On 30 January 1895 Msgr. Francesco Cassetta, Archbishop of Nicomedia and Almoner of His Holiness, wrote to Don Alfonso Baratelli asking him to inform the distinguished patient that the Holy Father granted him his blessing with the indulgence in articulo mortis. On 31 January 1895, at the age of 75, Fr. Giovan Battista Tornatore ended his earthly life: it was his dies natalis (= his birthday into heaven).

On hearing the news of his death, Archbishop Cassetta himself wrote a letter in which he stated: “From Fr. Agostino Donadio I used to hear of the great good this priest did by teaching theology at the Alberoni College in Piacenza, publishing treatises on Philosophy and Theology... directing the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne for many years, and promoting the cause of beatification of the Venerable Bernardo Clausi.”43

Divus Thomas, the prestigious periodical in which Tornatore published several of his works, wrote of him:

“This is how this most religious man spent his long life: in serving God, in study and in the practice of Christian charity; now in the heavenly homeland he will enjoy the reward. We trust that he will implore for us on earth the help of divine grace.”44

We reproduce the memorial concerning Tornatore recorded in the Libro in cui si contengono i Sigg. missionari Defunti in questo Collegio di S. Lazzaro, 1759-1904 in the Alberoni Archive.

It has the merit of offering a balanced and thoughtful reflection on the life and work of the Priest of the Mission, of bringing out objectively the figure of the man, the religious, the professor and the spiritual director, and of pointing to his tireless work for the cause of God and the good of humanity.

Culture and piety, learning and holiness, virtue and Gospel, the Vincentian charism and the gift of self to others: this is the background against which Father Tornatore, nicknamed the Saint, stands out.

m. In memoriam

1. Commemoration

“At six o’clock in the afternoon of 31 January, Mr. Giovanni Battista Tornatore, emeritus professor of Sacred Theology in this noble College, died of senile consumption at the age of 75. This most worthy Missionary was born in Dolceacqua, in the Diocese of Ventimiglia, to Bartolomeo and Rosa Campana, on 11 April 1820. Graced by the Lord with the spirit of holiness, throughout his life he was an angel in his conduct..., austere with himself, kind and accommodating with others. He was nicknamed Tornatore the Saint.”

“At the age of 16, having gone to Rome to visit one of his brothers, the late Mr. Domenico, a missionary student at the House of Montecavallo, he too felt called to become a missionary and entered the Congregation on 20 December 1836. In Rome he did his novitiate and studies with the spirit anyone can imagine. Having finished his studies and been ordained a priest in 1844, he was assigned by his superiors to the direction of students and to teaching. In 1852 he was sent to this College as Director of the missionary students and Lecturer in Sacred Scripture, posts he held from March to November. In November, at the beginning of the academic year, he was appointed Lecturer in Dogmatics and, alternating every three years between teaching Dogmatics and Moral theology, he remained a professor until 1877.

As confessor in the College and in other religious communities, Mr. Tornatore instilled his spirit, which was that of Saint Vincent, in all who came to him. With his Superiors’ permission he dictated the rules and saw to the direction of the New Foundation of charity called the Daughters of Saint Anne, an institution which owes to him its beginning, direction, growth and the good it is doing in the world. In 1893 he also devoted himself to the direction of the so-called Institute for the Scrofulous, founded in Piacenza by Msgr. Pinazzi, who bitterly mourned his loss, declaring that he owed to him all that the city enjoyed of his work.”

“Old by now, not so much in years as from the labors he had borne, he was being consumed by slow senile consumption, and at the beginning of 1895, completely exhausted and confined to bed, after receiving visits from the Bishop, from sisters, secular priests, rich and poor, whose tears were the finest tribute to him, he died on 31 January, as was mentioned at the beginning. His body was laid in the new Cemetery, in Niche No. 12. One of our Brothers who was caring for him related that on the last day of his life, while he was giving Mr. Tornatore some refreshment, he saw him gaze fixedly at a point in the room: his face seemed radiant with joy, and he pointed there with his hand with such delight that, the brother asserts, Mr. Tornatore was certainly seeing something that greatly consoled him.
