The Piacenza daily paper announced his death on 1 February 1895 with the following note, which we believe to be by his former student Don Gaetano Tononi: A precious life has come to an end at the Alberoni College. It is Fr. Giovanni Battista Tornatore, who died yesterday surrounded by his Confreres and some former students, after being blessed by His Excellency the Bishop.

Fr. Tornatore was very well known not only in Piacenza but throughout Italy and in the most reputable theological and philosophical Academies. As professor for very many years at the College of San Lazzaro, he helped give our Diocese its ablest and most learned pastors and directors of souls, in whom it takes pride. As confessor in the same College and in other religious communities, he instilled his spirit, which was that of his Vincent de Paul, both in the students of the College and in many other priests who turned to him.”

“Fr. Tornatore was a learned man and an ascetic. As a learned man he published various works, among them a much-praised one on the august mystery of the Most Holy Trinity. He also wrote several pamphlets in support of his theories, which he had rooted in his soul and turned into nerves and blood, and he wrote the finest pages that until yesterday adorned the «Divus Thomas», a theological and philosophical periodical published monthly at the Alberoni College, unique of its kind, which more than once received the high approval of the Holy See and of scholars in the most distant regions.”

“As an ascetic soul, Prof. Tornatore deserves, rather than a quick mention dashed off in a newspaper, a detailed biography written with love, in which, for the edification of all but especially of priests, ample mention should be made of his continual union with God; of his adorations before Jesus in the Blessed Sacrament, often lasting whole nights; of his Masses celebrated with a fervor one reads of only in the Saints most favored by grace; of his charity, his humility, his resignation even in the face of the assaults and hard trials God is wont to permit in order to test ever more the strength of his chosen ones and make their merit and triumph more radiant.

With all this, Prof. Tornatore had, we dare say, a youthful and cheerful character and was the most pleasant and delightful company. Austerity with himself, kindness and indulgence toward others: that is the character of the Saint. And Father Tornatore was such! The former students of San Lazzaro know it, who for half a century have always heard him called Tornatore the Saint. And they, the former students first of all, will certainly not fail to offer prayers for the soul of this excellent Missionary, to hasten for him, should he need it, the possession of Paradise.

Yes, rest in peace, good and holy son of Vincent de Paul, and from on high remember your dearly beloved Superior Mr. Manzi, your other confreres in religion and all those whom by word and example you guided toward learning, virtue and goodness.”45

2. Testimony

It is worth recalling at this point some simple, fresh episodes that remind us in some ways of the Little Flowers of Saint Francis.

They have kept alive in tradition Father Tornatore’s spiritual outlook and have brought out some of its features of capital importance. While allowing us to approach Tornatore’s personality, these episodes convey great lessons on Christian perfection and trace out examples to follow. They point strongly to the aitia (= the origins), so important for living today and looking to the future. In this respect it is essential to know how to combine past and future.46

- Devotion to Mary

Three days before his death, when he was so exhausted that he could no longer help himself, I went into his room toward evening and he said to me: “Dear son, what will Mary Most Holy say of me, since today I have not been able to say her rosary?..”

In his free time he always held his rosary in his hand and did nothing but honor Mary with this practice so dear to her sweet Mother’s heart.

In 1886 we made a journey together as far as Paola. On this long train journey he did nothing but pray the Holy Rosary whenever he stopped talking with me.

On this occasion we visited the Shrine of Pompeii. He stayed there the whole morning and, both before and after celebrating Holy Mass, he seemed in ecstasy.

With his eyes fixed on the picture of Our Lady, he saw neither who came nor who went. One can say that he saw nothing there but that picture.

At Montecassino, which we also visited, he seemed more a man of heaven than of this world.

All night, except for two hours (we slept in the same room), he stayed in prayer, and very early in the morning he went to the crypt where the bodies of Saint Benedict and Scholastica are kept; there, after praying for a long time, he said Mass at the altar of the crypt, and while he celebrated he seemed a true seraph.

In Naples we also witnessed the miracle of Saint Januarius. How beautiful it was to see him pray to hasten the liquefaction of the Blood! Kneeling on the altar step of Saint Januarius’s chapel, he did not move at all for 52 minutes, and his posture and bearing impressed those present too.

He was a friend of Cardinal Sanfelice; we visited him several times, and I saw how highly His Eminence esteemed him. As we left, the Cardinal also gave Mr. Tornatore a corporal that Fr. Bernardo had used when celebrating Mass in Naples.

At Paola we stayed three days. Those good Fathers gave Mr. Tornatore as his lodging the room where Fr. Bernardo Clausi had died.

Custom has no say when the Church speaks.

Saint Vincent did it that way then; but if Saint Vincent were alive now, he would do what the Pope says; indeed, if the Pope had said to Saint Vincent, ‘Take your Daughters and throw them all into the sea’, he would not have waited a moment to do it.

“Ah!” he would conclude, “whoever does what the Pope says is never wrong.”

- Poverty

His poverty always amazed me. He was truly detached from everything, and in an extraordinary way.

He gave no thought at all to his clothes, which had to be changed for him by force when they were torn or dirty.

For him everything was fine.

In his room he had nothing but a few books he needed for his studies.

If he was given something, he had given it away almost before he received it, often without even looking at what it was.

- Reading hearts

It was commonly believed that Mr. Tornatore could see into the depths of hearts.

Sister Celestina Ossola, Superior of the Vittorio Emanuele Hospice in Piacenza, a soul wholly given to God who was directed by the servant of God, told me a month after Mr. Tornatore’s death: “I am ready to swear that once, while I was in spiritual direction with Fr. Tornatore, he looked at me and revealed to me things I had within me which I know no one knew but God.

I cannot tell you what I felt then; it really seemed to me that I was before God’s judgment seat.”

Other people told me they were ready to swear that the same had happened to them, among them Mr. Salvatori, P.d.M., and the present writer.

- Chastity

Mr. Tornatore loved this beautiful virtue so much that one might have said he was rather excessive regarding this sin.

I noticed that when he was being shaved he took every care that the barber should not uncover his neck more than necessary.

When ill he was most careful to keep himself well covered, and if for some need the blankets had to be moved aside a little, he at once tried to be properly arranged again.

When cases of conscience concerning the sixth commandment were put to him, he adopted a very particular attitude, and in answering he was as brief as he was exact, clear and sure.

In conversation with people of the opposite sex he was not at all awkward, but one noticed in him a more reserved and dignified bearing than usual. He admitted sisters to spiritual direction only on their knees, and he always spoke to them holding his little holy picture in his hand, with his eyes fixed on it.

- Charity

If Mr. Tornatore was a man of intellect, he was no less a man of heart, and of great heart; his love, shaped by the charity of Christ, was the driving force that led him to perform so many works of charity.

The poor sufferers from scrofula also engaged him in all this. He always thought of the poor.

If in certain years the harvests were poor because of bad weather, he at once thought of the poor, saying: “How will the poor people manage this year!”

He collected alms for the poor and gave them to them. At times he might have seemed a nuisance, but he could plead the cause of the poor so well that one had to give.

When he went to a community he would go straight to the chapel to visit Jesus, and on coming out he would ask whether there were any sick and go at once to their bedside to comfort them.

In the college, when there were sick people, he never let a day pass without visiting them; and in the last months of his illness, when he could no longer get about, as soon as I entered his room he would ask me about the sick and want to know every detail of their condition.

- Death

On 31 January ’95 at midday he asked for the Sacrament of the holy oil, which he received with every religious feeling, himself answering the prayers of the rite.

Around two o’clock he received his last visit from Msgr. Scalabrini. Entering the room, the Bishop said to him: “Mr. Tornatore, what do you wish?” And he replied: “Monsignor, nothing but Jesus Christ.”

They then spoke alone, and Msgr. Scalabrini later said that they had understood each other very well and that he was very happy and greatly consoled by that conversation.

The last time Msgr. Scalabrini saw Mr. Tornatore he asked him for a keepsake to bear always in mind as a good rule for his life, and he told him: “Keep these words in mind: Adore - Be silent - Rejoice.” Msgr. Scalabrini later gave a conference on these three words to the Sisters of the Mother House in Paris when he went there after the feast at Clermont.

a. Wife, widow, religious

The figure of Rosa Gattorno stands out in the second half of the nineteenth century, joining the great personalities who gave impetus to religious life, considerable growth to the life of the Church and a particular mark to the human family.

Listening to the Spirit and docile to his inspirations, Mother Gattorno brought to life an Institute that reads the Bible in its own way and radiates it in the world with simplicity and kindness, with witness and service, with self-offering and compassion toward all who are in need.

Rosa was born in Genoa on 14 October 1831 into a deeply religious family. She was the second of six children, three boys and three girls, to whom must be added a half-sister her mother had had from her first marriage. Her father Francesco Gattorno and her mother Adelaide Campanella gave a firm direction to Rosa’s human, social and religious development and laid solid foundations in her heart.

Soon the city of Genoa and all Italy would be shaken by political upheavals that would later even bring about new arrangements with harmful consequences. A maternal uncle, one Federico Campanella, belonged to Young Italy and succeeded in drawing one of Rosa’s brothers, Federico Gattorno, into revolutionary schemes and Masonic ideologies.

At 21 Rosa married Gerolamo Custo; she gave birth to three children and faced serious trials. Financial ruin, rather grave illnesses and then the death of her husband and of her son Francesco seemed set to shatter the family and with it Rosa’s character and very existence. But she showed that she could face life with fortitude, courage and abandonment to God’s will.

She acquired a fair degree of culture, knew French, was skilled at embroidery, and sang and played quite well.

From her earliest years she was intent on knowing God’s will and on discerning the thread of Providence in the various events of life. With the help of her spiritual father she was better able to distinguish the voice of God from human voices.

Balanced and strong, prudent and practical, sensitive and attentive to the demands of the Spirit and to people’s real needs, Rosa lived her vocation as a Christian wife, welcoming all that was good, beautiful and noble and rejecting what was morally negative. Along these lines she worked out her spiritual journey, harmoniously combining the natural with the supernatural, nature with grace, making the most of the gifts and talents she had received and of her personal responsibility.

Widowed after only six years of married life, she opened herself more and more to the action of grace and to the plan the Lord was preparing for her: a plan sought in the darkness of faith. It was a mysterious design that Rosa approached through the mediation of the Church, prolonged prayer and very harsh penance. In this way she grasped the hierarchy of values, put God in first place and came to realize that God alone suffices!

To him, then, the primacy, to him the first service, to him full obedience and availability. Translated into life, this meant sacramental practice, ascetical exercise and a life marked and characterized by the charity of Christ, expressed in helping those in need. In short, we can say that, albeit in embryo and not yet completely clearly and definitely, all this lay at the basis of the new vocation that was taking shape on the horizon.

And so from 1858 Rosa Gattorno became more fully aware of the one Good and discovered the need to live according to the demands of the Gospel, the program of the beatitudes and the Sequela Christi (= the following of Christ) proper to religious life. Thus she passed from married life and widowhood to consecration through vows and to the foundation of the Congregation of the Daughters of Saint Anne.

The inspiration was shown to her more clearly in 1861, when she came close to the Franciscan world and discovered in the Poor Man of Assisi an example of life, a truly valid and significant model. Like Francis, to praise the Lord; like Francis, to proclaim the wonders of God; like Francis, to show compassion by caring for the leper.

From listening she moved to reflection, and from reflection steeped in prayer she opened herself to the divine in order to embody it in practice. That practice has a single name: charity, with its double meaning of love of God and love of neighbor. The neighbor takes shape in the person of the brother or sister in difficulty, in all those who, going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, fell among robbers and were left lying there alone, sick, groaning, crying for help. Above all they are the sick to be cared for day and night and served in the role of nurse, or girls in danger to be rescued, or children to be taught and brought up in the way of life and religion.

Rosa thus identified some dramatic emergencies of her time and intervened in person, gave a concrete response and practically drew up a manifesto. In 1864 she received the inspiration to found a work. In 1865, bound by her Bishop to carry it out, she asked to be able to speak to the Pope.

The encouragement of Pius IX and of Bishops Ranza and Scalabrini of Piacenza, and the support of many prominent figures of the time, would comfort her in making certain courageous choices and in undertaking activities marked by the risk of prophecy.

Her field of action: the roads of the world; her center of radiation: the church and the encounter with Jesus in the Eucharist; and then her little room as the place of her inner martyrdom, her self-offering and her union with her Crucified Lord, with the Trinity, with Mary Most Holy and with Saint Anne.

“She prayed lying on the floor with her arms stretched out in the form of a cross.”47 As Moses on the mountain, with arms raised, offered unceasing prayer for the people in battle, so Rosa Gattorno would spend whole nights keeping vigil, praying and imploring God for the work she had begun.

And on 8 December 1866, the solemnity of the Immaculate Conception, the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne was born, while she postponed her own clothing until the Feast of Saint Anne, 26 July of the following year.

The work had grown in her heart and conscience as well as in her hands! The benefits were immense, and very many people benefited from them. Clearly the new Institute needed much backing and support, collaborators and people who would bear its weight with her, organizing, structuring, changing and planning. Many people were involved in it and made themselves available for its varied needs.

In Rome Rosa Gattorno had the joy of meeting Pope Pius IX personally in a private audience on 3 January 1866. It was a meeting that represented encouragement and a seal of approval for her and her work. The Pontiff blessed her, encouraged her and entrusted her with a very simple but extremely significant message: “God will take care of your children: you take care of God in his work!”48

Rosa saw in these words a mandate and at the same time a testament of the Vicar of Christ, and therefore an obedience that admitted neither delay nor hesitation. She consequently made the decisive choices to respond positively to this invitation-precept and, though with martyrdom in her heart, in spite of misunderstandings, slanders, envy, jealousy and divisions, she would willingly take on even exhausting labors in order to serve the Church, the sisters and the poor.

In many cities of Italy she would find priests ready to lend her a hand and support her on her spiritual journey. She would show affectionate gratitude to all, although she would not feel able to make anyone’s activity or religious outlook absolute.

For Rosa felt overpoweringly the voice and inspiration of God, leading her along rough and often humanly inexplicable paths.

Of very particular importance would be Father Giovanni Battista Tornatore, with whom Mother Rosa succeeded in giving her work a structured form and her charism a concrete expression.

Father Tornatore, perhaps forcing things a little, moved with the Bishop’s consent into the sisters’ building in Piacenza in order to devote himself entirely to directing the Institute and to the all-round formation of the sisters. He wrote the famous Rules, the constitutive Charter to be presented to the Congregation to request its approval, drew up some circular letters together with Mother Rosa, organized the life of the Institute itself and took measures to keep discipline intact.

Having taken the work to heart, he assumed its direction (and in some way its fatherhood too) and shared its fortunes. And as happens in such situations, his strong presence was not always welcome, nor to everyone. Far from it! For this reason he would have much to suffer and would necessarily have to apply to himself the words of the Gospel: “Unless the grain of wheat dies, it cannot bear fruit.”

And Mother Rosa Gattorno? She let him do it! She was not in the least interested in titles or honor; she was interested in the service to be rendered to all, in working for the cause of God and of her brothers and sisters. Fr. Tornatore and Mother Rosa would have to face difficulties like mountains, very heavy humiliations, slanders, misunderstandings, discrimination; in a word, a journey of cross and martyrdom. But for them all this would mean not flight, estrangement or alienation, but full trust and hope in God.

Both were sustained by faith and both were aware that “if they persecuted me, they will persecute you too” and “when I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all people to myself”.

And Rosa Gattorno, now Mother Rosa Gattorno, united with the Mystery of Christ, truly draws people.

The Institute overcame serious problems and crossed national borders after opening a great many houses in almost every region of Italy.

What was the secret of its spread? This is the question historians ask, and many religious of our time ask it with great anguish when they see the decline in vocations and a certain complacency of life with regard to the founders’ charism. It is the question the Church asks herself today and puts to the world, and she seeks an adequate answer by scrutinizing the signs of modern times.

It is certain that authentic Gospel living, the clarity and splendor of the charism, a balance between consecration and mission, or more explicitly between inner life and activity, and the Mother’s wise guidance were fundamental factors in its growth and spread. To this must be added the great demand for work in the health field, then extremely deficient, as well as in education, and for a real response to the needs of so many girls in difficulty.

Within a few years the Institute presented itself to the Church and to the world with figures showing the extraordinary expansion of the work.

“At the end of 1873, after only seven years of life, the Daughters of Saint Anne numbered more than 200. Foundations multiplied: 6 in 1874; 6 in 1875; 10 in 1876; 12 in 1877; and so on, at an average of 10 Houses a year.

Its range was now wide: central Italy, Piedmont, Liguria, Lombardy, the Veneto, Sicily.

Before Rosa Gattorno’s death Sicily alone would count 60 Houses of the Institute, 15 of them in Palermo.”49

Passing through Rome on her way to Naples to begin a new foundation, the Servant of God was received in audience by Pius IX, together with the eight Sisters accompanying her.

“Here are the Daughters of Saint Anne, my ragamuffins,” the Pope exclaimed with a smile. He chatted kindly with them and gave them some advice: “Be apostles and be vigilant, for the devil does not sleep: often call upon Saint Michael the Archangel; he will defend and help you, and with his help you will do a great deal of good.”

When the Servant of God died in 1900 she had founded 318 Houses in Italy, 43 in America and 7 in Africa: 368 Houses in all, with 4,000 Daughters of Saint Anne.50

Meanwhile her sufferings did not end; rather, the way of sorrows opened wide. She lost some of her supports, first of all Father Tornatore himself, who was also removed from the Institute after having worked and sacrificed himself so much for the newborn work.

She would also have to endure some defections on the part of a few superiors and some sisters. And Rosa was there, ready to study and face the new problems and to devise new solutions.

The government of the Institute, which had now become a large family spread across continents, occupied her day and night. And she, having widened the scope of charity, thought of everyone and showed everyone the way to follow.

In April 1885 she was received in audience by Leo XIII: the Pope spoke with her at length, asked for news of the Institute and showed himself very pleased with what the Daughters of Saint Anne were doing in the world.

This time too Mother Rosa expressed her gratitude to the Lord for the grace of having spoken with the Roman Pontiff.

In 1881 the General Chapter, convened at the wish of the Ecclesiastical Authority, did not accept the amendments to the Constitutions proposed by the Holy See, the most important of which was the election of a general council.

With God’s help the foundress endured the stern reproof of the Cardinal Prefect of the Congregation of Bishops and Regulars. In a humble letter she acknowledged the fault unintentionally committed, and the chapter’s decision was retracted. It all ended with a letter from the same Cardinal praising the full submission of the superior general and her council to the dispositions of the Holy See.51

And before the end of her life came one more painful trial: the apostolic visitation of the Institute, begun on 28 July 1898 by the Benedictine abbot Dom Domenico Serafini on the orders of the Cardinal Prefect of the Congregation of Bishops and Regulars; it had been prompted by certain unfounded accusations of administrative irregularities and by the printing of the volume Travagli e conforti, which had been denounced to the Holy Office.

When the visitator presented his credentials and told her the purpose of the measure, Mother Rosa could not control her emotion and said in tears: “I already know that I am good for nothing, that I spoil everything: so I resign here and now...” Then, encouraged by Dom Serafini himself, she recovered and collaborated with him with complete sincerity. A month later, on 30 August 1898, thanking the community of Piacenza for their homage on her name day, she gave a very beautiful address to the sisters and said, with a clear allusion to the trial she was going through:

“Yes, love the Mother, love her in holy Church... Daughters, I want one promise from you today: that you be faithful to the Institute and to holy Mother Church. No, daughters, let not slanders, troubles or anguish make you fail in your holy vocation... I too was slandered, despised and ill-treated: and not even the slightest thought against my holy vocation crossed my mind.”52

Perseverance and constancy, then, fidelity to the Institute, that is, to the charism, and fidelity to the Church. This seems to be the key element and, as it were, the significant feature of her testament, dictated by a heart that was most clear-sighted and martyred.

On 10 February 1900, while the apostolic visitation was still in progress (although the clouds had been dispelled), Mother Rosa fell ill, and on 6 May she completed her holocaust. God’s work had been accomplished in her! And Rosa Gattorno, her eyes and mind turned to God and her arms stretched out to her brothers and sisters, left to the Church and the world a spiritual heritage of the greatest importance and a many-sided project, to be considered both in its beginnings and in its troubled course, to whose fulfilment heaven and earth, God and man, contributed.

b. Guided by the Spirit, enlightened by people

From the day of Pentecost until the Parousia (= the last times) it is the Spirit, God’s gift to his pilgrim people, who guides and leads the Church, and at the same time it is the mediation of the Church that gives direction and offers the light needed to move toward the good and live the Christian life to the full.

The action of the Spirit, then, as the foundation and constitutive reality of the Church, and the activity of the human person placed in perfect harmony with the Spirit, on the same wavelength. In a word, the mystery of a soul that searches out God’s loving plan, that seeks the Lord’s ineffable light and every day, through a process of interiorization and the vicissitudes of human life, must read the will of God!

The history of spirituality constantly speaks of the need for spiritual direction and thus for the spiritual director, a figure that over the centuries played a leading role and that today, for various reasons, sadly seems almost to be disappearing. Spiritual direction has in fact broken down for various reasons, some essential, others because of certain methods no longer suited to or accepted by modern people.

In her passionate search for God and his will, Mother Rosa Gattorno truly made use of many people, whom she approached with humility and openness, in a spirit of obedience and with great docility, while knowing that she must not and could not sacrifice her freedom and the inspirations coming from the Spirit. For this reason she would face many difficulties arising from the temperament, human outlook and spiritual ideas of those who wanted to support her on her journey.

The problem of spiritual direction would therefore be one of the most persistent sufferings in Rosa Gattorno’s life.

While still a girl she opened her heart to the priest Don Antonio Accinelli and asked his advice before marrying.

Later she asked to be guided by Don Giuseppe Firpo, custodian of the metropolitan church of Genoa. Meanwhile her situation in life had completely changed!

After her husband’s death Rosa found herself having to face life alone, look after the family and deal with a thousand human, social and financial problems.

Widowhood has always been a terrible situation! It certainly was for her too. Don Firpo took on with great responsibility the task of directing Rosa Gattorno; he would moderate her program of mortifications and seemed at once to sense the extraordinary response Mother Rosa wished to give the Lord. He therefore understood the work the Spirit was doing and Rosa’s inner struggle, and he willingly cooperated with this generous soul.

Differences of outlook and difficulties of understanding must certainly have weighed heavily in her decision to give up the help offered by Don Firpo. Moreover, Rosa flatly refused to submit to the exorcisms he had proposed in an attempt to free her from certain diabolical vexations. Already in 1861 Rosa experienced loneliness, complained of it to the Lord53 and prepared herself in suffering to look for another director.

“In 1864 she had begun to go to confession to Don Luigi Cogrossi, with the Archbishop’s consent; this priest had a reputation for holiness, and Rosa had gone to see him in his home town, Castelleone, in the diocese of Cremona. Don Cogrossi later accompanied her to Rome, when she was received in audience by Pius IX, and introduced her to various prominent people in church circles.

The Servant of God relates how, on her return from Rome, determined to begin the foundation of the Institute in Piacenza, her confessor, probably Don Firpo, disapproved of what she had done.54 The matter ended happily at the beginning of 1867 when Rosa, now a foundress, renewed her filial relationship with her former director.”55

Rosa Gattorno would continue to use Don Cogrossi’s help in Piacenza too: he served both as chaplain of the new community and as its ecclesiastical superior until he was removed in August 1867.

From 1870 Fr. Agostino Donadio of the Order of Minims would make his valuable and significant contribution, offering his wise and enlightening spiritual counsel and also helping in sound discernment, both to guide Rosa’s conscience and to give light to her budding institute. Mother Rosa, however, did not choose him as her spiritual director.

Another Father, Fr. Bernardino of Portogruaro, came on the scene in 1884. He was a learned and holy priest, a religious who had even been minister general of his congregation and had launched a great renewal within his order. Rosa thought she had at last found her spiritual director.

Things did not turn out that way, however: her meetings with Fr. Bernardino caused her no little disturbance and anxiety, and even scruples and discouragement with anguish. Nonetheless Mother Rosa tried with all her strength to open her soul fully to this Father General, but as she herself declared, “no direction satisfies me, however learned... I cannot adapt...”56

In 1885 she formed with Don Gennaro Granito Pignatelli di Belmonte, whom she had already met in Naples in 1877, a deep spiritual friendship that would become ever stronger and more vibrant. Her last confessor would be the Capuchin Fr. Vincenzo d’Alatri, who assisted her at the hour of death and supported her in the last months of her earthly life.

Meanwhile, from March 1866 Mother Rosa had had the opportunity to know and appreciate Fr. Giovanni Battista Tornatore, a priest of the Mission, quite well known and esteemed in Piacenza and elsewhere for his great and wide theological, moral and juridical learning and for the holiness of his life. He was a man particularly versed in the things of the Lord and passionate about his vocation: a person who lived his specific calling to the full, zealous for the worship of God and versed in the science of the Spirit.

An excellent judge of the human heart, he willingly and very generously advised Mother Rosa, sacrificed himself for the new Institute and became so involved in her cause that he took on a truly decisive and in some respects irreplaceable role.

Despite their differences of character and experience, Mother Rosa and Fr. G.B. Tornatore complemented each other: together they made plans, together they faced the problems that beset them daily, both signed certain documents addressed to the superiors and communities, and together they dealt with the constant emergencies in which the Institute lived.

“The role he played in guiding the foundation has earned him recognition by the Daughters of Saint Anne with the title of co-founder.”57

Fr. Tornatore’s merits with regard to the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne are indeed very great! He believed in Mother Rosa, had full confidence in her, in her uprightness and in her passion to consecrate herself to God and place herself at the service of the poor. So he sacrificed his time and let himself be drawn more and more into Mother Rosa’s project.

For this reason he endured very hard trials within his own religious community: humiliation on the part of the Congregation, together with being pointed at by the religious world, the human community and society.

To all this must be added a difficult relationship with Mother Rosa herself, who soon realized that their characters were incompatible.

So with Fr. Tornatore too the spiritual relationship was not plain sailing. She listened, accepted his direction and conformed to the Father’s will and opinion, but always in faith and overcoming very considerable obstacles.

At this point we may fairly ask: why so many spiritual directors and not just one? Why did Mother Rosa so suddenly change holy and devout people who were doing their best to meet her spiritual needs? Was it a trait of character that could not be overcome, or must we look for other explanations, perhaps on a higher plane? Was it the rather authoritarian manner of spiritual direction that was being called into question, or direction itself?

Mother Rosa let herself be guided by the Spirit and by those who helped her grow in freedom of conscience and in obedience to the voice of God and the Gospel of Christ.58

Clearly all the spiritual Fathers Mother Rosa turned to, Father Tornatore included, found themselves before a very special person with an extraordinary mandate. Faced with her adoption of the prophetic criterion, her readiness to take risks for the Lord, her interpretation of the Gospel sine glossa, her going beyond certain juridical norms (= human logic), they all showed perplexity, raised doubts or, at best, fell back on prudence and expediency, or tried to delay and postpone matters to another time. But when zeal consumes... when charity urges... the need of one’s brother cries out to our conscience! Mother Rosa, amid constant torment and perpetual conflict, said: “We must obey God first and then men,” and then, trusting fully in her Lord, she prayed and declared her full readiness: “Ecce Domine mitte me!” (= Here I am, Lord, send me). Yet she did not hide her unease, the difficulties of the journey and the need often to decide without the comfort and support of her spiritual Father.59

In hindsight it will certainly be easier to grasp the thread of Providence and better decipher the history of Salvation as it takes flesh in human history. All these priests lit a small flame or even a torch to light Mother Rosa and her path, while Christ, the Light of the world, and his Spirit guided the life and mission of the Foundress from within.

c. United by a single program

Once the insight is there, practice follows!

Within this dialectic, understood dynamically, lie the whole many-sided program of the Daughters of Saint Anne and the whole work of Fr. Tornatore.

But clearly this was a typically prophetic project, a broad and complex program of life that required every day the light of faith and the fervor of charity.

Reform must be put into practice through one’s life before it has actually come about. Here the term reform has many facets, including the idea of woman and the role she can take on in society, human advancement, evangelization, physical and moral care, and the whole theological and spiritual framework of each consecrated woman, and so on.

As a result: difficulties, problems, misunderstandings, haste for results seen from the standpoint of human logic! On the other side, the impulse of the Gospel, the call of the beatitudes and a constant appeal to compassion and forgiveness.

Alongside the way of justice, Mother Rosa and Fr. Tornatore followed the way of charity. In this the project was one: Mother Rosa’s charism was fully shared and promoted. The charity of Christ urged them on and allowed no hesitation, delay or postponement. Duly spurred on, they worked tirelessly; their arms multiplied!

After a few years the Institute grew, developed and expanded and, breaking through national barriers, went abroad to America.

In the Circular of 1880 we read:

“The foundations established number nineteen; nine of them have already opened, and the other ten will open shortly. Among these new houses, one has been founded in America, in Bolivia, beside the one already there: in this new House a school of 80 girls is being educated in Religion. In addition, negotiations are under way to open three more in America too, in three different cities, to which 40 sisters would be called.”60

In a creative way, then, the aim was to embody the Gospel among the people of the time: poor and weak women carried out impressive works that astonished people, aroused wonder and enthusiasm and contributed to the transformation of minds and still more of hearts. When the Daughter of Saint Anne approaches with her simple, motherly smile, it is Christ who approaches, God who visits, the Spirit who calls, transforms and sends forth to bear witness. The love of Christ is indeed contagious: it spreads like an oil stain, reaches even the most distant hearts and leads them back to the Good. The presence of the Daughters of Saint Anne means the spread of a new culture, a culture of peace and joy.

The very image of the sister speaks of the presence of the divine, recalls the spiritual, and carries forward, explicitly or indirectly but really, the program of evangelization and holiness.

Now, all this cannot be improvised! It is the fruit of prayer and study, of experience and sensitivity, of listening to God’s voice and of availability to the Church.

d. From charism to institution

The charism suggested to the Church by the Spirit needs an institutional form!

This is an obligatory step: the charism must be ratified by authority. No group, movement or association can call itself Catholic, and thus fully in line with the Church, unless the Church recognizes it as such. The same applies to all initiatives that arise within the Church.

We realize that such a process often meets considerable difficulties, sometimes misunderstandings too, with the resulting sufferings that lead along the way of the cross and martyrdom.

Yet in spite of this crucible, the process of institutionalization has always been required and is the basic aspiration of every Christian. We might say that it is a true common denominator shown down the centuries by all who have opened a path of works and spirituality in the Church and for the good of people.

For this reason all founders and foundresses are obliged to draw up certain Rules and give them a significant role, so as to keep God’s gift constantly alive, express it fully and impart to it a lasting dynamism.

The task is particularly demanding and calls for constant updating and renewal, while always keeping authentic and true the gift of the Spirit and what has been entrusted to the Church.

Mother Rosa Gattorno had received directly from Pope Pius IX the order to write the norms and so set out the main lines of the work, which was becoming ever more consolidated. But she was made above all for life and for carrying out concrete works of charity for those in need. Humility, the real difficulty of undertaking a truly demanding task for people without qualifications, fear of making mistakes and of failing to capture in words the genuineness of the project, together with the great confidence she had long placed in Tornatore: these were certainly some of the reasons that led the Mother to entrust him with drawing up the Rules. But to this must be added a supernatural motive that always runs like a thread through Mother Rosa’s life and work: her special relationship with her Lord, her Beloved, with Saint Anne, and also her converse with Fr. Bernardo Maria Clausi.61

In this way Mother Rosa thought she had at last solved the problem, which seemed to her every day more difficult and urgent.

Fr. Tornatore accepted the invitation and, with his characteristic generosity, set to work at once and completed the task in a few months. It was a simple work that embodied Mother Rosa’s project and brought into focus the special features of her charism; a work that described plainly what was to be carried out, what the basic spirituality of the sisters was and how the Institute was to be structured; a work that set out the very coordinates of religious life: consecration and vows, apostolic activity and government, style and character, formation and asceticism, commitment and responsibility, care and sensitivity toward the poor, and so on. Mother Rosa was most grateful to Father Tornatore for his work and felt that she had thus fulfilled the task entrusted to her. Moreover, the Father’s experience and the relationship that had united them for some time seemed to guarantee success!

In February 1868 Mother Gattorno handed the manuscript of the Rules to the Bishop of Piacenza, Msgr. Antonio Ranza, and had a second copy delivered to Cardinal Consolini. Having obtained the oral approval and consent of the Bishop of the Diocese, Mother Rosa at once had the precious booklet printed and distributed it among the sisters.

The Bishop had expressed himself favorably, so the longed-for approval was as good as given! Moreover, Mother Rosa believed in conscience that the guidelines set down in the Rules, and in particular the teaching on piety, the virtues, prayer, charity, fraternal life and apostolic commitment, were of great significance and substantially matched her own ideas. So she decided to write to Cardinal Quaglia, then Prefect of the Sacred Congregation of Bishops and Regulars, to inform him of these Rules and request their approval.

The Mother herself probably thought it was almost a formality and a permission more or less taken for granted, given the opinion of the Bishop of the local Church and the credentials of Father Tornatore, a cultured religious of holy life, quite well known among the philosophers and theologians of the time.

The Congregation, however, after reading those Rules, issued a very severe judgment and rejected them; moreover, it ordered Mother Rosa under obedience to withdraw and tear up all the copies in the house at Piacenza and in the other houses.

It was 19 February 1872. Such a verdict sounded like the destruction of the work and consequently the annihilation of the people who had enthusiastically and passionately consecrated themselves to God and to the service of others.

With a bleeding heart Mother Rosa obeyed and without delay set about carrying out fully what she had been ordered. God’s plan follows a logic other than that of men. On this occasion too, though she did not understand, Mother Rosa showed her full submission and complete readiness to do the will of the Hierarchy.

Reasons of orthodoxy, communion and authentic spirituality, and criteria of ecclesial belonging, require the approval of a new Institute by the Hierarchy.

The charism must therefore be received and sifted before being taken up by the Institution. In this way it is submitted to the judgment and discernment of the Church.

A simple woman, she would never have thought that the approval would be so troubled and difficult, so complex, and that it would put her own religious life and the course of the new institute to so very severe a test.

Rome imposed an obedience that would have knocked anyone out: all the copies of the Rule written by Fr. Tornatore, already circulated in the various houses, had to be torn up immediately!

Her world fell in on her! The project seemed truly compromised... and yet she had done her very best and had also exercised sound discernment: everything seemed to be falling into ruin and ending miserably!

This news came like a bolt from the blue; what is more, it seemed humanly inexplicable. How painful it is for anyone to have to taste the mystery of suffering and drink the bitter cup of misunderstanding!

With a torn heart Mother Rosa obeyed, kept her faith alive and renewed her trust and abandonment in God. If this was his work, he would have to see to it. Meanwhile she set about carrying out that peremptory order and gave instructions for all the copies to be truly destroyed.

It was a delicate moment: many sisters clearly had difficulties and did not understand, others considered the measure unjust, and the Bishop himself was at a loss. She, however, was entirely ready and wanted the order carried out without any delay and without batting an eyelid!

e. The reasons for the rejection

Why did the Roman Congregation reject Tornatore’s Rules and even order them to be destroyed?

Did they contain doctrines contrary to the faith and morals of the Church? Certainly not! The truth of faith was in no way in question, nor was moral conduct. The problem lay elsewhere, in the style, form and novelty of the charism. Blessed Giacomo Cusmano would meet similar difficulties when, at roughly the same period, he sought approval for his Institute called Il boccone del povero (The Poor Man’s Morsel).

The Rule usually presented to the Congregation was drawn up according to precise, rather spare canons and in a juridical tone.

Fr. Tornatore, on the other hand, had set out his text in the form of a dialogue and, moreover, as an inspired account, as if it were a continuous heavenly manifestation or a vision indicating the project step by step and tracing out the way.

It was certainly only a matter of method, but one that already indicated at least a different outlook and above all an unusual approach.

Added to this was the name Daughters of Saint Anne! But the title did not convince the consultors. At that time everyone honored the Saints, Anne included, in an ordinary and traditional way, whereas the Rule proposed a different and highly original cult. Anne was presented as a living presence, not according to tradition: a presence that pointed to a spirituality and required imitation in the various circumstances of life.

As we have already observed, Fr. Tornatore sided rather with those who described Saint Anne as the Mother of Mary Immaculate and at the same time as an extraordinary element of continuity between the Old and New Testaments. It is Anne who receives Mary, the Mother of the Redeemer, and opens herself to the new history of Salvation, while also representing an essential link with the ancient history that begins with creation, passes through Abraham and the remnant of Israel and reaches its culmination in the person of Christ Jesus.

Saint Anne therefore plays a wonderful role in the mystery of Salvation, and the Daughters of Saint Anne are called to embody it, after Mary’s example, in living their vocation.

This way of conceiving spirituality, however, was a novelty at that time. And Rome then had great difficulty with, not to say an aversion to, novelties! Modernism was raging, devastating and unhinging everything. Hence the determination to maintain and defend traditional doctrine and orthodoxy, and to spread the Gospel according to well-tried teaching!

In such situations it is precisely the most markedly prophetic proposals and the new ways of embodying and living the Christian message that pay the price.

That is always the way! What is traditional and well tried creates no great problems, whereas the new and renewal necessarily involve risk and uncertainty, doubts and worries, even when the new comes from reliable people. The experience of Francis of Assisi is emblematic in this regard, and 1968 has something to teach us.

The distinction between the absolute and the contingent is difficult; and it is always possible to make absolute what is merely tradition and custom, answering to the criterion “we have always done it this way”!

The problem of the Rules, despite the order to destroy them, remained open.

On 4 December 1871 Msgr. Wanstienkist informed the Mother of the decisions taken in Rome concerning the Rules: the ecclesiastical authorities were to withdraw them from whoever had them, so that the printed copies might be torn up.

On 1 December 1872 the same Msgr. Wanstienkist, on behalf of the dicastery, let it be known that if the Rules of the Dorothean sisters were adopted for education and those of the Stigmatine Sisters for the running of hospitals, there would be no problem.

But Mother Rosa could not accept this substantial change, because what was at stake was the fundamental charism, the constitutive and founding inspiration of the work. She therefore felt she could not give up her Mother: “They want to take my Mother from me,” she wrote in her secret notebook. “No, a thousand deaths, but save the Mother!”

This very simple expression shows how strong her love for Saint Anne was and how firmly she held to the project, the charism and the spirituality flowing from it.

She therefore could not give up the distinctive character that was to be the identity card of every Daughter of Saint Anne.

Prayer, witness, consistency of life and the strength of conviction, which splits rocks and carries all before it, broke through and brought about reflection and a real review of the case.

At the same time the dicastery’s severity and harsh stance toward Tornatore, who had been ordered not to concern himself with the Institute and the Daughters of Saint Anne, began to soften. The Mother had been tireless and had tried in every way, through letters, appeals and talks with Msgr. Salvatore Vitelleschi, to have Fr. Tornatore reinstated in the Institute and allowed to resume his work as spiritual director and former of consciences.

Msgr. G.B. Scalabrini, the new Bishop of Piacenza, vouched for the Lazarist Father, and Cardinals Vannicelli in 1874 and Berardi in 1876 authorized Tornatore to rewrite the Rules and to return to forming the sisters. The storm over drawing up the norms to be submitted for Rome’s approval had also struck hard at him personally, for he had been practically removed.

It was 1876 and everything began again from the beginning. 1879 would be the year of the approval of the Institute and of Fr. Tornatore’s readmission to his former role.

A good five years had passed since 19 February 1872: five years of suffering and misunderstanding, five years of darkness and of the crucible, lived by Father Tornatore in silence, in prayer and in faith.

In 1885 the Holy See approved the text of the Rules ad experimentum for 10 years, and on 26 July 1892 Cardinal Verga, Protector of the Daughters of Saint Anne, would hand Mother Rosa the definitively approved Rules.

So ended the troubled journey that had involved practically everyone who, directly or indirectly, had the fortunes of the new Institute at heart: the Bishop of Piacenza, who had arranged for their circulation and application in his diocese; Mother Rosa, who had committed herself to living them and helping others live them; Fr. Tornatore, who had spent his best energies translating a splendid charism into writing. Nor can we forget all those who, in a spirit of great collaboration, had worked according to the guidelines proposed by both Mother Rosa and Fr. Tornatore.

The very complex affair of the approval of the Rules, and thus of the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne, by the Congregation of Bishops and Regulars produced an abundant correspondence, already studied from different angles by Francesconi and Iriarte and earlier by Fiocchi.

We note that this correspondence forms a web, at times clear, at times obscure, among the parties concerned. Onto the scene, and consulted in various capacities, come Mother Rosa Gattorno and Father Tornatore or the other drafters, who longed for the Holy See’s ratification; the consultors, who formed their opinion on the basis of the documents submitted; the Congregation as such, charged with this most delicate task; and the Bishop of Piacenza, Msgr. Ranza and then Msgr. Scalabrini, as guarantors of the gifts and ministries the Spirit gives to the local Church.

Such a web easily leads to considerable difficulties, delays and misunderstandings, or prompts calls for a certain freedom of action. And if the bishop’s assessment does not fully agree with the mind of the Apostolic See, then trouble ensues for all, and everyone is in effect obliged to clarify matters and retrace their steps to review and examine the question.

It is the Church as a whole that sets out on a search and carries out an extraordinary task: obeying the Spirit.

That is what it is all about! Only the Spirit must never be stifled or quenched, not even when the process of transformation must begin and the charism must be codified. More than that, the Church’s authority must responsibly welcome the novelty proposed and hold it up to the Christian people and to the world as a model of life.

But let us retrace, with the help of the documents and with reference to the authoritative voice of Bishop Scalabrini, the course that led to the approval of the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne.

1866. The city of Piacenza benefits from the services offered by the Daughters of Saint Anne.

“This city also enjoys the contribution of the Daughters of Saint Anne [...], who assist the sick in their homes day and night and take in, teach, clothe and feed poor boys and girls. Rosa Gattorno of the Diocese of Genoa laid the first foundations of this worthy association in this city of Piacenza in 1866: with spiritual and material help the Society soon grew and spread to various Dioceses of Italy; here, besides the Mother House, in which the most devout Foundress resides and exercises the office of Superior General, it has opened two other houses and a fourth in the village of Castellare.”62

1876. The Daughters of Saint Anne received the Decree of Praise from the Sacred Congregation of Bishops and Regulars. They nevertheless remained under the protective authority of the Bishop of Piacenza, because the Rules written by Father Tornatore had been approved by Msgr. Ranza but withdrawn and burned in 1872 on the orders of the Holy See, which required Tornatore himself to be removed.

1876. Together with the Decree of Praise some observations for modifying the Constitutions were sent to the Bishop. Mother Rosa hastened to send the Rules to Bishop Scalabrini, saying: “Your Excellency will make whatever changes you think fit.”63

1879. On 21 April the same Sacred Congregation sent the decree of definitive approval together with further observations to be made to the Constitutions. Mother Gattorno, however, never learned of these observations and consequently did not see to amending them as required.64

Bishop Scalabrini asked Rome for instructions and was charged with exercising a special protective authority over the new institute in both spiritual and temporal matters65 (although he too never had the first observations in hand).

1881. On 17 March Cardinal Ferrieri asked Scalabrini to convene, if he thought fit, a General Chapter of the Daughters of Saint Anne in order to give Mother Gattorno a general council, a body necessary when important decisions have to be taken. The Mother showed herself willing.66

1881. In August the general chapter was convened under the presidency of Scalabrini himself, but it unanimously rejected the Congregation’s observations, considering them harmful to the Institute.

The Bishop took note of this but at once reassured the Holy See of the sisters’ obedience. Mother Gattorno and the general Council appointed on the orders of the Sacred Congregation retracted what had been done.67

Meanwhile, for some years misunderstandings had been creeping into the relationships between Scalabrini and Mother Gattorno, between Mother Gattorno and Tornatore, and between Tornatore and the Congregation.

But let us try to shed some light on the matter using Francesconi’s excellent study.

“Some clouds passed over the relations between Scalabrini and Mother Gattorno, first of all because of the usual conflicts of authority between the Bishop, who had been charged with exercising protective authority over the Institute, and the Cardinal Protectors, who disregarded the task given to the bishop. In the dispute with the Archbishop of Florence, Msgr. Cecconi, who in 1878 wanted to remove the Daughters of Saint Anne from Florence, Scalabrini wrote to the Secretary of State:

‘I am most grieved that the excellent Archbishop of Florence has declared himself so vigorously against those poor sisters. As I told Your Most Reverend Eminence, there are some blemishes (and where are there not, in human institutions?); some sister may well have failed, but the general spirit is excellent and could be much improved once the rules are approved and the most devout and learned Tornatore has returned to his office.’

But the Substitute, Msgr. Cretoni, replying that he had obtained from Msgr. Cecconi a postponement of the Sisters’ removal, did not fail to observe:

‘I could not say Msgr. Cecconi is wrong, if his complaints about a certain spirit of independence from the Ordinary, of which the Sisters in Florence are said to give proof, are well founded.’

A similar impression might be gained from a letter of Scalabrini to the Prefect of the Sacred Congregation of Bishops and Regulars:

‘For those Nuns the Bishop might as well not exist. They turn to me only for some trouble or, at most, for some minor function. The deepest mystery surrounds that House. It is like a beehive, with people constantly coming and going. The one who does everything, or lets everything be done, is His Eminence Alimonda, their Protector, on whom alone they declare themselves dependent. I know nothing at all, because I am informed of nothing [...]. If I am to have responsibilities regarding that Congregation, I should like to know what my powers are in the matter. If it all comes down to providing the Confessor, so much the better.’”68

We know that Mother Gattorno, though with some reservations and perplexity,69 had placed herself in Fr. Tornatore’s hands ever since meeting him in Piacenza in 1866. It is in this light that we must read:

a. the task given him of writing the Rules (1867);

b. his appointment as administrator, spiritual director and almost superior (1867);

c. her warm appeal to Bishop Scalabrini, to the Superior General of the Vincentians and to Cardinal Patrizi not to remove him from Piacenza (1870);

d. her many attempts to rehabilitate him and restore him to his office;

e. the task of rewriting the Rules;

f. the direction of the various houses and the task of organizing them.

Therefore, when in 1872 Cardinal Vannicelli ordered Fr. Tornatore to be removed from the Mother House and forbade him to hear the sisters’ confessions, Scalabrini intervened, partly at Mother Rosa’s urging, and asked Rome to restore the spiritual direction of the Institute to Tornatore, clearing him of the charges of heterodoxy:

“Having summoned and strictly examined him, We have found him sound in the philosophical, theological, moral and ascetical sciences, so that in justice We must declare mistaken, and as such reject, the judgment of some who, moved by zeal but lacking due knowledge, had defamed him as being in error; therefore We, on the basis of certain knowledge of the facts, declare and attest that the aforesaid Giovanni Battista Tornatore, Priest of the Mission of Saint Vincent de Paul, Professor of Theology at the venerable Alberoni College and administrative director of the Daughters of Saint Anne, as above, is eminent for integrity of life and conduct, so much so that he is commonly known by the name of saint.”

In a later declaration, attesting “the very great spiritual and also material benefit” brought to the diocese by the Daughters of Saint Anne, he added:

“We therefore trust that an even greater benefit may be hoped for, and We desire it and will continue to desire it from the Lord with the most ardent affection of heart, that he may deign to send, through holy Mother Church, a man after his own heart for the spiritual direction of this worthy Institute. On this subject We consider it superfluous to express Our feeling once again, since so far We have nothing to add to or remove from the testimonials We issued earlier on account of anything that has happened in the meantime.”70

On 4 March 1876 Msgr. Francesco Tammi, Vicar General of Bishop Scalabrini, wrote to Mother Gattorno informing her “confidentially” that in January he had received definite news of the mind of the Cardinals of the Sacred Congregation of the Inquisition on the Tornatore affair. The Roman Dicastery clearly stated that it “rejected for ever, without any hope either for the present or for the future” any request to readmit Fr. Tornatore to the Mother House in Piacenza as spiritual director. The Mother had in fact repeatedly asked that the Father be restored to his usual role. Mother Rosa, for her part, pointed out (and she spoke from direct experience!) how valuable the Father’s collaboration had been for her houses and for the formation and spiritual direction of the sisters. And not only that: she herself asked the Priest of the Mission for advice.

“From all of them I came away truly edified. But it was above all in the Mother House of the daughters of Saint Anne, founded not long ago by the most devout Lady Mother, Anna Rosa Gattorno, that, together with great edification... And how could I not be distressed to hear that a House which a few years ago could comfortably support itself and help four other Houses likewise founded in this Diocese, two in Piacenza itself and two in Cortemaggiore (in which five Houses a full 450 girls receive the instruction they need), is now reduced to the utmost poverty? When I asked those Sisters the cause of this decline, I was told: the removal of Mr. G.B. Tornatore, Priest of the Mission, from the direction of this Mother House, ordered by the Holy Office.”71

Fr. Tornatore’s removal did indeed impoverish the Institute from every point of view (spiritual, organizational, financial and so on).

“That is why I beg you, Monsignor, to permit Mr. Tornatore to be restored to both the spiritual and the temporal direction of this Mother House. I said spiritual direction, because those he directs can only derive the greatest benefit from it; I added temporal direction, because with Mr. Tornatore’s recall those frequent and abundant subsidies that he, with his powerful and numerous connections, knows how to obtain for it will also return to the Mother House, and since his removal they have unfortunately almost entirely ceased! And I will further observe that the lady foundress has done and continues to do, as they say, the impossible, running here and there to provide as best she can, but, not to mention the general scarcity...

That being so, Monsignor, I beg you once more that, to satisfy the wish of my Bishop, my own and that of the daughters of Saint Anne, Mr. Tornatore be allowed to resume the Direction of their Mother House. Such a concession, I assure you, will directly benefit those daughters and indirectly the Diocese.”72

In truth the removal had probably taken place only in part, because the Vicar General Tammi had not immediately put Rome’s decision into effect and was studying very diplomatically how to face and solve the problem.

“I kept the Sacred Congregation’s letter strictly secret and allowed Mr. Tornatore to continue his office in the Mother House (though I myself never, never, never saw Mr. Tornatore again), resolved to tell the matter only to Your Reverence once you were back in Piacenza and to agree with you on what to do. When, four or six days ago, the Bishop told me ‘that he had summoned Mr. Tornatore, had him tell the whole painful story, examined him minutely on the principles of Philosophy and Moral Theology, seen his Diploma as a member of the Academy of Saint Thomas, that Tornatore is in Rome, and finally that he wished to send a testimonial to Rome in Mr. Tornatore’s favor’ - oh! then I thought it necessary, for the matter to proceed well, to show the Bishop the letter of 13 January, so that he might see to whom, in what terms and when to send the testimonial, so as not to clash head-on with the Holy Roman Congregation. The Bishop then told me about Cardinal Berardi and the two sick women cared for by the Daughters of Saint Anne, showed me and left with me Your Reverence’s letter and the other from Mr. Tornatore, and ended by charging me to prepare the testimonial, which I shall have ready today; the Bishop will sign it and send it to Cardinal Berardi, so that he may forward it to whoever is most appropriate.”73

What settled the question was in fact Bishop Scalabrini’s testimonial, in which, after describing in a few effective strokes the work of the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne, he went on to highlight Tornatore’s personality, focusing mainly on his orthodoxy, his piety, his moral teaching fully in line with the doctrine of Saint Alphonsus Maria de’ Liguori, his obedience to the Church’s hierarchy and his devotion to the Roman Pontiff, and concluded by asking that he be restored to his particular functions within the Institute of Saint Anne:

“... through the zeal and industry of our beloved sister in Jesus Christ, Rosa Gattorno, author of the Association... with what fruit for souls and progress of young girls in the true faith, piety and religion...

And since from appropriate information We are certain that the Very Rev. Don Giovanni Battista Tornatore is endowed... and has for many years been Rector in temporalibus... and having been examined by Us... diligently and strictly in the Lord, We found him wise in the philosophical, theological, moral and ascetical sciences, so that We should rightly consider mistaken, and as such reject, the judgment of some who, moved vainly by zeal but not by knowledge, defamed him as having fallen into error...

... We certify and attest that the aforesaid Fr. Giovanni Battista Tornatore... is so distinguished for integrity of life and conduct that he is commonly known by the name of Saint, for his piety, religious zeal and very great devotion to the Holy See and the Vicar of Our Lord Jesus Christ; praiseworthy for all the other virtues befitting a churchman, able in intellect and learning, a follower of sound principles in the philosophical disciplines, a Thomist in Dogmatics, a Liguorian in moral Theology and, in ascetics, opposed to condemned mysticism, so that he deserved to be numbered among the members of the Academy of Saint Thomas Aquinas established in Rome and approved by the authority of the reigning Supreme Pontiff Pius IX, as We can attest from the diploma of his admission delivered to Us...”74

1879. Fr. Tornatore was entrusted with the oversight of the daughters of Saint Anne.

1880. Fr. Tornatore received the delegation to visit the houses of the Institute, and by a decree of 27 February 1880 he was appointed “Director of the Mother House of the aforesaid Institute in this city and its co-founder”; and in 1883 Msgr. Scalabrini again turned to the Holy See to have the ban on the Lazarist hearing the Sisters’ confessions lifted: “Fr. G.B. Tornatore, founder of the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne, is a most distinguished churchman in every respect [...]. It often happens, Your Eminence, that the good Sisters of Saint Anne, when mortally ill, wish to open their souls and make their confession to this Father of theirs, whom they venerate, and rightly so, as a Saint, and one always has to invent a thousand pretexts to deny them that grace which would be the greatest of their comforts.”75

Scalabrini calls Father Tornatore “Founder of the Institute”. In truth this title had been suggested by Mother Rosa out of humility, expediency and diplomacy, in order to give the Institute more credibility, to overcome difficulties more easily, to find solutions and to share the burden and responsibility. We should bear in mind the culture of the time and its ideas about women and the tasks a woman religious could take on.

Fr. Tornatore, for his part, continually brought the matter back to its proper course and repeated to everyone, especially to the Sisters, that the Foundress, the Superior and the Mother General was Rosa Gattorno.76

1880. Fr. Tornatore was effectively rehabilitated.

1888. Immediately after the General Chapter, Father Tornatore, excluded from the Institute, definitively lost the rights of direction he claimed and believed to be within his competence.

In July 1981 the daughters of Saint Anne fulfilled the Father’s often expressed wish “to have on my tomb a little dust trodden by such heavenly daughters”, and moved his mortal remains from the cemetery of San Lazzaro Alberoni to a small chapel beneath Mother Gattorno’s room in the Mother House in Piacenza.

“The events described did not prevent Scalabrini from showing full confidence in the Daughters of Saint Anne: in 1879 he entrusted to them the new Institute for Deaf-Mute Girls; on 1 June 1884 he crowned the image of Our Lady Mater Gratiae et Misericordiae in the Mother House; he sent them to New York for the first hospital founded by his missionaries for emigrants; he asked the Foundress for a directress and a novice mistress so that the new Missionary Sisters of Saint Charles for emigrants might learn ‘the free and modern spirit’ of the Daughters of Saint Anne; he was several times a guest at the Generalate in Via Merulana in Rome; and he contributed decisively to the favorable outcome of a financial dispute, freeing the sisters from paying a large sum of money, so that the superior general Mother Benedetta Carrega, who succeeded Mother Gattorno after her death on 6 May 1900, felt bound to express repeatedly ‘perpetual gratitude’ and ‘eternal thanks’, as well as the personal thanks of Cardinal Rampolla, the new Protector, for all the good the Bishop did for the Institute.”77

a. I too will boast!

A document of 1888 drawn up by Fr. Tornatore lists, in a terse and insistent manner, everything he had done for the Institute as founder and superior, and sets out at great length his “titles of superiority” with regard to the civil authority, the ecclesiastical authority and the Institute itself.

Titles of superiority over the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne before the civil authority.

“I took part as Superior of the Institute in all the contracts concerning the Institute’s interests, up to that of Signora Michelotti. A sign of this is that when the dispute arose between the Institute and Angelo Richini over the contract for the foundation of the house at San Pier d’Arena, I was summoned before the Courts, as was the Mother; I had to take oaths, and when Richini later sent defamatory writings everywhere, the first name to appear was Tornatore’s. Likewise Signora Michelotti, having repented of the contract made with the Institute, threatened first of all me, if her wishes were not met, that she would present me to the Sacred Congregation as a man who had induced her to the contract by crafty persuasion. It was then decided that I should no longer appear in contracts.”

Titles before the ecclesiastical authority

“At the meetings presided over by some ecclesiastical authority I was present at all of them as Superior of the Institute. The first was presided over by the Cardinal Protector and by His Eminence Laurenti, then a Monsignor, and dealt with how to return the dowry to a sister who had left the Institute. The second, also presided over by the Cardinal Protector, I attended as Superior. The third was the Chapter held by order of the Sacred Congregation and presided over as Delegate by the Bishop of Piacenza, and I attended all its sessions as Superior.

Titles within the Institute

The idea of the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne was mine; from me the Institute received the name Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne; the first daughters were clothed by me so as to give them the name daughters of Saint Anne, and the Mother accepted this idea and carried it out. The Rules were written by me. And when they were burned by order of the Sacred Congregation of the Holy Office, I rewrote them by order of the Cardinal Protector Berardi, so that the rules the Institute now has, both the common ones and those concerning all the offices of superiors, beginning with that of the general, were written by me. The Mother has stated all this a hundred times, both to outsiders and to the Sisters. At the time the Rules were completed and I was suspended from all jurisdiction, a letter came from the Commissary of the Holy Office in which he recognized me as Superior General of the Institute in temporal matters.78

I always exercised all the offices proper to the supreme Superior of an Institute. No houses were opened without my consent, no candidates were received without my consent, no one was assigned to an office without my consent. All the circulars sent every year to all the sisters are signed by me. In the foundations of the Generalate built in Rome (Mother Rosa) had a stone laid bearing the name of the Protector, her own and mine. One day, in my presence, Monsignor Graselli asked who I was; she answered: this is our Superior. I was recognized by the sisters as Superior of the Institute, and as such they always turned to me for advice. At the beginning of the Institute I judged both the outward aspect and the culpability of faults; later the Mother judged the outward aspect and I judged the culpability.”79

In the same vein is the letter sent to Bishop Scalabrini’s Secretary, in which he complains that Cardinal Alimonda calls him quasi co-founder:

“What? The Institute originated with me, because the idea was mine; it received its name from me; from me they have the name of Daughters of Saint Anne; the Mother was only the instrument for carrying it out, and now they will say quasi? [...]. I want it declared, yes or no, whether I am co-founder and Superior. That done, if ever through the wickedness of human affairs (which I do not believe) I cannot remain in the Institute, my son, without its being divided, like the child of the two mothers before Solomon, then I would rather withdraw.”80

The text calls to mind chapter 11 of Paul’s Second Letter to the Corinthians, in which the Apostle boasts of his weakness and of the gifts and many experiences that had accompanied his mission.

Elsewhere Tornatore himself seems to allude to this text and to use the same literary genre: “I play the fool,” he says, “in praising myself; but I am forced to it.”

Was it an outburst on the Father’s part? Was it a list of titles needed in order to draw up contracts, and thus motivated by legal necessity so that he would be qualified to do so? Or was it an apologia in his own defense against those, and there were certainly many, who accused him? Some considered him crafty and cunning, and so capable even of extracting wills and donations for his works. Some discredited his orthodoxy, considering his philosophical and theological teaching out of line with the Magisterium of the Church. Some did not look kindly on his tireless work in guiding Mother Rosa’s foundation.

All these titles nevertheless raise some doubts. They seem to us in truth exaggerated and in any case open the way to undue claims, even though the context and the difficult climate of suspicion may have played a part.

The exaggeration lies in the fact that everyone, the Pope, the Bishops, the priests and the people, unanimously recognized the charism as Mother Rosa’s, while she in her humility cared little about claiming the credit.

Yes, it is true that the Institute had taken a name different from the one first envisaged. But the Foundress herself had received the Name by the Lord’s inspiration. The contribution of mind and heart generously offered by Father Tornatore was in any case widely appreciated by all. Moreover, the collaboration between the two became ever fuller and in many respects binding. In this regard Mother Rosa would be constantly torn between a form of rightful autonomy and one of dependence.

It was she, however, who held the reins of the new communities, though she consulted others and accepted directives, guidance, suggestions and whatever else she considered useful for the Institute’s development.

It was she whom the Holy Father had asked to write the Rules, and she whom the Bishops asked to open new houses. To her, therefore, the title of Foundress fully belongs. On 3 January 1871 the Bishop of Piacenza, Msgr. Antonio Ranza, clearly set out the terms of the question, distinguishing between the role of Foundress of the Institute, which belonged to Mother Rosa Gattorno, and that of director, which he attributed to Fr. Tornatore.

“To support the earnest wishes of the Reverend Mother Anna Maria Rosa Gattorno, foundress of the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne opened in this City and directed by the Very Reverend Don Giambattista Tornatore, Priest of the Congregation... I venture to ask you kindly to receive the aforesaid Rosa Gattorno.”81

Correspondence signed by the Mother and with the Bishop’s consent then asked the competent authorities that Fr. Tornatore be removed from obedience to his local superior and made answerable directly to the Father General.

Fr. Agostino Donadio pointed out that Father Tornatore’s work for the Institute was certainly praiseworthy provided it was done in obedience to his superiors.

“I find everything in your letter praiseworthy, provided our dear Father can do everything with the due permission of the Superiors of his Institute; for if he took other paths than those of his own Superiors, our Father would in some way lose his reputation, and perhaps the Institute would suffer too. I think, my good daughter, that if the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne is the Lord’s work, all obstacles will be overcome; our good Father, without leaving his own Institute, will be able to give it greater luster and greater help. Meanwhile speak about it with the Visitor, tell him your ideas and see what he thinks, whether you can obtain that the Father be a little freer to devote himself to this new foundation, and after all that leave it in the hands of Divine Providence... I remain firm, however, in my view that our Father should indeed work for the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne without leaving his own, and the Lord will give him strength and light to bring the work to completion; it will be ever more to his glory and he will gain greater merit, and our most beloved Mother will give such a spirit of Fortitude, Wisdom and Holiness to the poor Daughter of Saint Anne that she will make her Institute advance on the way of perfection and Holiness.”82

And the Visitor and Assistant General replied in the negative on 13 February 1871.

“In your esteemed letter of 8 January you ask the Superior General that Mr. Giovanni Battista Tornatore be dedicated to the care of the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne, removing him from obedience to his Local Superior and leaving him subject only to the Superior General.

He has asked me to reply that such a request surprised him not a little, coming from the Superior of a Religious family, and that he regrets having to tell you that he cannot grant it.
