Mr. Giovanni Battista Tornatore is a Professor at the Alberoni College and may be called to other ministries, and however great the good he can do for your Institute, it is not the way of our Congregation for any work, however good, to be made exclusive. Moreover, removing him from obedience to his Local Superior would cause very serious difficulties both for himself and for the Community.”83

It is all too clear that Fr. Tornatore was in considerable difficulty and was trying to resolve it with the Mother’s help, either by detaching himself from his own Institute or at least by living only under obedience to the general.

Clearly the work truly weighed on him and its burden was heavy. Moreover, a great work does not come into being all at once and needs a thousand contributions. Father Tornatore, like Mother Rosa, was searching in the dark and may have mapped out wrong paths or launched projects that later had to be tested.

One might perhaps say that the charism is like an aircraft that the Spirit causes to take off. It (the charism) must then make the crossing, often through turbulence, and after contacting various control towers it must land. The aircraft may have several pilots, but what is decisive is its registration and flag. And registration and flag together speak one name: “Mother Rosa”.

Fr. Tornatore once again produced his credentials: professor at the Alberoni, expert in and defender of Thomist doctrine, obedient to legitimate authority. Victim of deceit and condemned in odium personae (= out of hatred for the person), he was forced to defend himself and to show that his work for the Church, for the College of San Lazzaro and for the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne had been carried out with personal commitment and responsibility.

“I therefore think it my duty to explain the reason to you. Here it is: in 1870 the Bishop of Piacenza, Antonio Ranza, of happy memory, approved the printing of the Rules of the Daughters of Saint Anne written by me. In 1876 they were presented in Rome, and the Holy Office proscribed them, because Monsignor Salua, under-assessor of the Holy Office, said they came from the Alberoni College, where there were ignorant Professors who did not know the doctrine of Saint Thomas; so they were forbidden in odium personae, as I shall now explain. The disgrace of the condemnation fell entirely on the Bishop, who had allowed them to be printed under his name; his distress was therefore great, and he told me to give some proof that Saint Thomas was studied in the College. It was then that I wrote the work entitled Commento dell’angelico dottore S. Tommaso d’Aquino de’ Predicatori alle due decretali d’Innocenzo III esposto e dichiarato dal P. Giovanni Battista Tornatore della missione. This work was approved by the Master of the Sacred Palace and reviewed by able Theologians, in particular by the periodical so renowned here in Italy, La Civiltà Cattolica. The Master of the Sacred Palace told Msgr. Salua that I was a profound expert in the doctrine of Saint Thomas; after this, those Rules which had first been proscribed were approved, and they are the ones the Daughters of Saint Anne observe. Now this work, while clearing me of the charge of ignorance of Saint Thomas’s doctrine, also cleared the whole College; and yet it was printed entirely at my own expense, and since I had to have it printed by the Propaganda Fide Press it cost me more than 700 (seven hundred) lire. This work was enough for the College to be cleared in Rome of the reproach of being an enemy of Saint Thomas, but the Seminary of Piacenza did not stop calling us false Thomists. The present Bishop brought out the Divus Thomas, and since it was the Bishop’s periodical, the Seminary too was invited to write for it.”84

He returned once more to the question of being co-founder in a letter that follows the same apologetic line and reveals all his bitterness and disappointment, even though he manages to express himself with some detachment!

“Now I want to make you laugh at an expression I read in that letter; it tells me: the Mother thanks you for your kind remembrance of the daughters of Saint Anne. It is laughable to thank a Father for remembering his daughters!... But we know already that Sister Anna Celsa says: Father Tornatore is not recognized by the Church as co-founder. But she must know that a fact and the recognition of it are two different things.

Saint Ignatius was founder and Superior of the Jesuits for thirty years before he was recognized as such by the Church, and the same may be said of all founders: Monsignor Gianelli, founder of the daughters of Mary dell’Orto, died without having been recognized. So the fact is a fact, whether recognized or not; it is a fact and no one can undo it.

If certain little sparrows now asleep were to wake up, they would bear witness to this fact; so would a certain letter whose signature bears two mysterious initials: if those two initials were explained, people would say Father Tornatore is not co-founder but arch-co-founder. When I presented to our Procurator General my titles as co-founder, in order to justify myself before my General (to show that when I had Monsignor Scalabrini, who is still living, write to the General, Fr. Etienne, that since I was co-founder and the Institute had grown, it needed my whole person and he should therefore relieve me of every office in the Congregation, I had not deceived either the Bishop or my General in writing thus), the Procurator told me: you have more titles than Saint Francis of Assisi. He named Saint Francis because he knew the Father General was doing everything he could to have him driven out.

These titles were titles within the Institute, before the civil authorities and before the Ecclesiastical authorities. These are the titles I presented to Monsignor Salua, who said, as it were: what? you climbed these stairs so many times to have me reinstate Fr. Tornatore, and now... And at once he drew up a certificate with the seal of the Holy Office, attesting that the Sacred Congregation had always recognized me as Superior General of the Institute, and he added: if this is not enough, I will make you another, fuller one.”85

b. Fr. Tornatore’s temptation

Religious are Christians who, answering the Lord’s call, consecrate themselves to him through the vows of chastity, poverty and obedience and, living within a community, conform themselves to Christ, embrace his Gospel radically, embody the beatitudes and point the world to the saving presence of the kingdom.

Are they then perfect? Certainly not! They are called to live perfection, but like everyone they experience trial, temptation and sin. The history of spirituality has clearly identified certain temptations that commonly make inroads into the hearts of religious: abandoning the state of life they have embraced, changing community and taking different patterns of behavior elsewhere, perhaps in search of other experiences.

Emblematic in this regard is the vivid description in the apophthegmata patrum (= sayings of the Fathers), which censure the restlessness of the early monks who pack their bags by day and then think better of it at night and unpack them!

No less harmful is the behavior of many religious today who think they must drink from the trickles of certain modern spiritualities, giving up or neglecting the one proposed by their founders and tested over many centuries. Too many today move from one Institute to another in search of a spirituality or values that they may find at the emotional level but not in terms of faith, and so not authentically.

The question does not arise in these terms for Fr. Tornatore who, having embraced the Congregation of the Mission, lived it with enthusiasm, fervor and gratitude to the Lord. He had worked well and given proof of obedience; he had taken a great interest in the cause of the Daughters of Saint Anne; then he asked to devote himself entirely to the Institute and to be exempted from obedience to the Superior of his community so as to be directly subject to the Father General.

The request was made directly by Mother Rosa, but we are led to believe it had his explicit approval. The reasons for it: greater freedom of movement, greater liberty to work for his foundation! Yet this is precisely what seems to have been at issue. The Congregation of the Mission considered it useful and even praiseworthy for Father Tornatore to work for the Daughters of Saint Anne, to look after their financial and temporal projects, to direct souls and instruct everyone in the way of God and holiness, but on condition that he remain a religious of the Mission and never be detached from the body to which he belonged.

The request will be refused kindly and courteously, but firmly, clearly and unambiguously. To leave almost always means losing one’s role, losing dignity and authenticity as well as credibility.

It was a wise decision that helped to shed some light on a matter that was undoubtedly becoming delicate and causing considerable unease within the Congregation of the Mission, among the Daughters of Saint Anne and in the Church at large. There must have been many who disliked his presence and his excessive zeal; moreover he managed a great deal of property useful and necessary for the development of the work, which evidently aroused the greed of many. The Roman Authority had even decided on his removal from the Institute, probably also to restore balance and enable Mother Rosa and her Institute to stand on their own feet and manage everything independently!

“Some time ago I mentioned the intention expressed by our Fr. G. Battista Tornatore of leaving the Congregation so as to be free to devote himself to promoting the good of the Community founded a few years ago and called the Daughters of Saint Anne... so it happens that for some time now, on days when he has no teaching, he goes into the city in the morning and returns in the evening.

Sometimes he needs to travel on urgent business for the Community. Since he sees that the Visitor and I are reluctant to grant him such permissions, and on the other hand he finds himself charged by the Roman Congregation with helping the Foundress with his advice and assistance, he has conceived the idea of leaving the Congregation in order to devote himself entirely to this work; he believes he has clear signs of God’s will and says he cannot withdraw, having already been committed to it by Rome. The Bishop, to whom he has turned for help in achieving his purpose, is unhappy about it and would prefer that he be granted, by way of exception, the permissions he needs so as to reconcile the one with the other, his assistance to this work with his duties as a Missionary.

I would therefore like to be more at ease and to be able to say that he acts with his Superiors’ permission. It would be enough to authorize the Superior to grant such permissions as are compatible with the duties of a Missionary. That would settle everything, and the Bishop would be happier.”86

The problem seemed solved, the request withdrawn!

The Superiors recognized Fr. Tornatore’s talent and charism and thought they could overcome the difficulties by granting him permission to act more freely. We believe, however, that Fr. Tornatore would be constantly in inner conflict and obliged to examine his conduct every day in order to reconcile the life of the Institute with obedience to his superior. Nor should we forget how utterly lost he felt after being excluded twice, in 1872 and 1888, from the work of the Daughters of Saint Anne. In practice he was constantly in conflict and probably had to face the mockery of certain zealous people who must have exclaimed: “We said so! We knew it! Serves him right! And he even wanted to leave his own Institute to follow...”

c. Father and Teacher

It is well known that devout and spiritual people, who carry out great works and vast projects, do not like to show off or to boast of or profit from what they achieve.

And Father Tornatore was certainly among those deeply religious people who devote themselves with Gospel radicalism to God, to Christ’s message and to the Church.

He believed in Mother Rosa’s charism at once, as Cardinal Dusmet believed in Don Bosco’s charism, inviting him to open a house in Catania, and Bishop Turano in that of Blessed Cusmano. Here, however, there was a difference: the work was promoted by a woman, and a widow at that! This was no small matter, given the typically male-dominated outlook that had prevailed for centuries and the fact that her religious vocation came from a different state of life.

All this must be stressed, because it was indeed a very considerable difficulty.

Fr. Tornatore, like Mother Rosa, with fine prophetic insight understood Mother Gattorno’s charism, welcomed it, guided it and supported it. More than that, he committed almost his entire life as a priest and Lazarist religious to the new work, made it his own and shared in it to the point of taking on, though gradually, the features of fatherhood.

His was indeed a vital sharing. Fatherhood and sharing, then: these would always be the two poles of Fr. Tornatore’s activity.

It was a fatherhood grounded in the ontological relationship with God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ; a fatherhood that is born and fulfilled only in pain and affliction. Just as the Church was born on Calvary from the pierced side of Christ asleep on the Cross, so anyone called to communicate the life of the Spirit, and thus to give life, can do so only by imitating the apostle Paul, who in his own life completed what was lacking in Christ’s sufferings for the sake of the Church.

Fr. Tornatore was the one who provided the conditions and prepared the ground so that the work could come into being, spread and bear fruit, building up the Church and spreading the fragrance of Christ along the roads of the world.

A father is one who loves the work he has promoted to the very end. Hence his attention and care, his solicitude and concern, his vigilance that everything should happen according to God’s plan, and his drawing up of the Rules to give solidity and to set a style of life.

Having to direct souls and learn “the art of arts”, the Father was called to mark all his actions and all his dealings with people with discernment and discretion. But all this requires patience and gentleness and a considerable store of human and psychological qualities.

This art is neither easy nor simple: history, people’s characters, adverse circumstances, misunderstandings and above all God’s plan put it severely to the test. Father Tornatore experienced all this and also tasted the bitter cup of being set aside and having to break with Mother Rosa and the Daughters of Saint Anne!

Like all Christians, Fr. Tornatore found it hard to grasp God’s will and to discern the situation of the moment; he could not understand how and why the Holy See took certain positions. The Mystery of the Cross visited him and invited him to submit to the passion and share in Christ’s suffering. But he never closed his heart:

“... I have lived,” Tornatore would say, “and will always live for the good of the Daughters of Saint Anne; and I feel more love now that they have put me out than when I was inside.”87

The bond had become very close: sustained by love for Christ and for Saint Anne, it overcame difficulties. It could not therefore be broken by any legal injunction, because it was founded on God’s own love, which is gratuitous. It was a charity that reckons with not being returned but does not for that reason halt its loving purpose.

Father Tornatore had to tread the path of self-offering so that the Lord might grant his help and favor to the work and above all to the people carrying it forward.

He was well aware, moreover, that no work can be accomplished without being united to the Crucified.

Yet Tornatore, full of faith, did not waver and kept his trust and hope in God unchanged even in the darkest moments. Like Abraham, father of believers, he went on hoping against hope. Whenever possible he always tried to clarify and explain, but he knew how to accept God’s will.

In the end, however, the obedient man will sing of victory; truth will triumph; good will prevail over evil... But at what price? At the price of blood and of the witness of martyrdom.

This attitude was neither flight nor alienation. Fr. Tornatore was always in the thick of things, always ready for dialogue and discussion, to enlighten and guide, available to direct souls and lead them to God. But he knew that one must also wait for the Spirit’s timing and for the resulting interiorization and maturing of people’s consciences.

Guided by the sound principles of prudence and enlightened by the knowledge and wisdom of Christ and his message, he would be called to give advice and pass judgment, running the risk of error, exaggeration or making absolute something that was really “a minor matter” and so not essential to religious life. And then there were the environment and culture of the time, together with traditions, which carried considerable weight!

Father Tornatore was a guide for Mother Rosa even when he himself had to be guided by her. Just as the Church is in Christ the Light and Teacher of the nations and yet has much to learn from them, so Fr. Tornatore was called to engage with and learn from Mother Rosa, from her insights, her journey, her experiences and the directives of the Church given to her, as well as from the orientations arising from the Communities of the Daughters of Saint Anne themselves.

Fr. Tornatore was Teacher for the novices and the professed sisters and set out for them the lines of spirituality, the charism, the style and the direction of the Institute.

Letters very often reveal a person’s true spirit and disclose, between the lines, secrets, passions and aspirations as well as difficulties and suffering. Tornatore’s correspondence, still preserved and jealously guarded, covers a fairly long span of time, from 1852 to 1894.

In these forty years he used letters to give biographical news and to speak about the Alberoni College (teaching, orthodoxy, organization) and financial difficulties. Of great interest are the letters dealing with the life of the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne (the course of the Rules, relations with the Congregation of Religious, with his superiors and with the bishops of Piacenza). Particularly important are those written to the Sisters.

They show a simple and serene relationship, as well as an enlightening and wise one.

We quote a rather significant and illuminating extract that clarifies his relationship with Mother Rosa and the role of each within the Institute, and brings out the spiritual dimension.

Writing to Sr. Paola Bucciotti in Genoa in 1871 he says: “I also remind you that when the Mother instructs you on any point, you must obey her promptly, because she has supreme authority over the whole little Institute: she is recognized by the Pope and by the Cardinal Protector of the Institute as Foundress and Superior General, and, as the Rule says in Chapter 7, No. 1, p. 67, it is to her that the sisters make their vow of obedience. It is true that she wishes to depend on my advice in everything and does not breathe without depending on me; she does this out of love for obedience, and in this she is certainly admirable; but even without me she has authority to do in the Institute whatever she thinks right: to receive sisters or not, to send them away, to found houses, and so on.”

From this correspondence emerge the soul and the struggle of Fr. Tornatore: a priest committed to guiding people and leading them to the Lord.

And when he was no longer to concern himself with the Institute, would he cease to be its Teacher and Father? Certainly not!

All who knew him are well aware that he remained an example and model for many. The events that went against him reveal the human condition and thus bring into better focus, alongside the lights, the shadows that inevitably occur within a church community.

But this will certainly not cancel out Fr. Tornatore’s most valuable presence and tireless work, both for the daughters of Mother Rosa who began the Institute with her and for the generations who will follow her, embodying the same gift of God.

d. Heart-rending obediences

1. Withdraw all copies of the Rules
2. Remove Fr. Tornatore
3. Punishment through calumny

Modeled on Christ, religious life can only express itself in total obedience to Christ, to the Spirit, to the Church and to one’s superiors.

Together with chastity for the Kingdom and poverty, obedience is therefore constitutive of religious life and is the way to go to God,88 to anticipate the eschaton (= the last times), to live according to God’s plan and to build up the community. In practice obedience must become the very life of consecrated persons.

The history of spirituality emphasizes in this regard the commitment of every religious to live his or her vocation constantly in faith and to believe firmly in the Church’s mediation, in the role of the superior in pointing out the way of obedience as an indispensable means for the spiritual life and thus for progress in perfection.

The Second Vatican Council rightly set out lines of updating and renewal regarding certain outdated ways of practizing obedience, but it reaffirmed the theological content that Scripture and Tradition have always asserted.

Mother Rosa and Fr. Tornatore had embraced the doctrine of obedience in a spirit of faith and had long practized it and shaped their lives by it. Consequently, like Christ, they would often be called to drink cups and taste all their bitterness.

In lives already wholly marked and firmly characterized by obedience, there were certain episodes and certain acts of obedience that may rightly be called “heart-rending”.

By way of example we recount three acts of obedience that left an indelible mark on the conscience of both, certainly laid a stone in the building of their spirituality and gave impetus to their growth as Christians and as religious.

1. Withdraw all copies of the Rules

The “bureaucratic” process became more and more difficult and complex. The Mother really thought the matter should be concluded as soon as possible. So, rushing through every stage, she gave a copy to the Bishop of the Diocese, who, knowing the new work quite well, welcomed and applauded it. But it would not be so in Rome. The Congregation even passed the document on to the Holy Office, because it saw in it certain things that, in its view, simply could not be accepted. More than three years went by and nothing came. But in the end the peremptory order arrived to withdraw all the copies and tear them up.

Mother Rosa, deeply grieved, hastened to carry out this dramatic obedience. Sensitive as she was, she was truly distressed also by the penalty inflicted on her Father Tornatore.

The Rule burned, fruit of love, discernment and service to the Institute, and like victims of sweet fragrance their hearts, their security and their stability burned with it.

An abyss seemed to open before them: “What shame,” the Mother wrote, “I suffered together with my secretary! I no longer had the courage to show my face anywhere!”

Yet she, or rather they, would have the courage to obey and to anchor their trust in God, who would surely provide!

A hope with no evidence, a hope against all appearances!

2. Remove Fr. Tornatore

Trust accompanied by esteem lies at the root of any true and constructive dialogue and involves communications that are expressions of life, outpourings of one’s soul and experience.

Added to this is the awareness of the concern the other person has shown: a concern for me and my life!

It is in this light that we must read the relationship between Mother Rosa and her Institute and Father G.B. Tornatore. He had gathered the little flower of the field and made it grow and develop; he had taken great care of it and spent himself for everyone, organizing and supporting, comforting and encouraging, taking an interest in each one and, when necessary, taking risks and paying the price himself.

His extensive correspondence with a great many sisters clearly shows his kindness, attentiveness and sensitivity. The sisters were happy when they could write to Father Tornatore, talk with him, meet him and open their hearts. Likewise for Mother Rosa, Father Tornatore was a support, especially in the early years of the Foundation. She could always count on him, sure of not being neglected or ignored.

For many years Father Tornatore had shown that he spent his life for the people and for the Institute as such.

The Holy Office’s order to “remove the author of the Rules” was a terrible obedience for Mother Rosa. And as if that were not enough, Father Tornatore was also to be removed and kept away from any involvement in or direction of the Institute!

But on this occasion too both of them, Fr. Tornatore and Mother Gattorno, though they did not understand and though they sweated blood, bowed their heads, accepted and submitted, and in humility and submission showed their fidelity to the Church and declared themselves ready to obey, that is, to be crucified like Christ Jesus.

3. Punishment through calumny

The Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne had scarcely been born and already, sadly, there were defections and evil designs. Among these was a calumny against Mother Rosa. It was the end of March 1869 and Mother Rosa was in Sampierdarena, already very worried about her son Alessandro, who faced the amputation of a leg.

On receiving a letter, she left at once for Piacenza.

She arrived at Piacenza station at 11.30 p.m. At midnight she was knocking at the door of the Mother House. She was kept waiting and then there was even reluctance to open to her. Once inside, she asked for the Superior, surprised not to see her. She was told she was in bed. Not having the key to her own little room with her, she went up to the Superior and asked first of all what was the matter, whether she was ill. She received a curt no. The other Sisters who were with her stood there silent, with an air of mystery and embarrassment.

“But what is it? Why are you so upset?” the Mother asked.

No one answered: only the cook, who had followed her closely ever since she came in, pressed close to her, saying under her breath: “Mother! Poor Mother!”

But no one bothered to break the ice. No one thought to offer her anything or to invite the Mother to rest. The night was bitterly cold and Rosa, chilled to the bone, then asked to be given a room where she could retire. She was told to go to the guest quarters.

Rosa Gattorno then withdrew to the chapel and stayed there all night.

Morning came at last. She received Communion and, after her spiritual exercises, went to the Superior.

“What is it?” she asked her. “Speak.”

“I don’t know,” she replied.

“What? And where is Mr. Tornatore? When he comes, call me.” The Superior shook her head and murmured: “He is not coming; he will not come any more.”

“What?... But what on earth is the matter?”

At last Father Tornatore, after being sent for several times, sent word that he would come toward evening, but not to stay.

He came, entered the parlor, called Mother Gattorno and at once forbade her Holy Communion. He mentioned some very serious accusations made against her by the Superior, and left.

“I wept a little,” the Mother says at this point, “then, reflecting on what those accusations were about, I became calm. But thinking that for fourteen and a half years I had never once missed Holy Communion, I felt great pain. I obeyed. In the evening, in my dear poor room, I scourged this monster of a body.”

The next morning at nine Father Tornatore came to hold a kind of trial, and he held it in the place where the Sisters usually made their confessions. It consisted of two small rooms connected by a little grille. On one side sat Tornatore, in whose presence the Servant of God stood; on the other, in turn, were those who had made the accusations. The Father read aloud a very long statement that took a full five hours, from nine until noon and from one until three. Mother Rosa listened on her knees.

In the afternoon, while the reading of the accusations against the Mother was still going on, the cook suddenly burst into the room. She broke into tears and began to protest: “The Mother is innocent... it is all a conspiracy...”

On the other side of the grille another Sister threw herself on her knees and, weeping, begged forgiveness, saying: “The Mother is innocent... It was the Superior who forced me to sign...”89

Only then did Father Tornatore realize that he had fallen into a trap, perhaps out of naivety or perhaps through the professional bias of a moral theologian. Saint Alphonsus de’ Liguori, too, had believed certain calumnies against Gerard Majella and had deprived him of the Holy Eucharist, imposing excommunication on him.

Mother Rosa did not rebel; she accepted and, in tears, generously offered her forgiveness, thus showing the greatness and nobility of her heart. Fr. Tornatore apologized for the incident, and his esteem and appreciation for Mother Rosa grew stronger.

a. Novelty within an established heritage

Historians maintain that the second half of the nineteenth century produced no significant novelty in the field of spirituality!

“The trends in spirituality,” writes Gregorio Penco, “may seem, in this second half of the century, of little significance or prominence, having produced no great spiritual author and no truly original school. More than at other times, the isolation in which the religious world found itself seems to have prevented the kind of deepening and development that could bear comparison with other periods and schools. The spirituality of this period is largely represented by the founders of the new religious Congregations, who became its teachers in their respective institutes, at times in extremely difficult circumstances. This explains the close bond strengthened in this period between personal charism and institution, as well as the somewhat generic character spirituality itself took on.”90 Other historians of spirituality take the same line.

“At first sight the trends of Christian spirituality in the second half of the nineteenth century may seem of little significance, having produced no exceptional leaders or inspirers of schools as in previous centuries.”91

Above all there is a lack of great masters, of outstanding figures who develop spiritual teachings and treatises on spirituality, that is, works that mark a turning point, as had happened for example in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries.

The drive toward practice and the strong weight of tradition thus underlie Christian living. Hence the development of a spirituality with eclectic and syncretic features.

An eclecticism and syncretism of wide scope and with very interesting implications. Consequently there was no decline at all in Christian living, since commitment and efforts at interiorization were to be found everywhere.

In this period the validity of forms of popular devotion was re-examined, the Feast of the Sacred Heart was extended to the whole Church and the worship of the Eucharist was promoted. “Finally, with the definition of the dogma of the Immaculate Conception of Mary (8 December 1854), the Marian movement rapidly flourished again in all Catholic countries and, supported subsequently by the encyclical Ineffabilis Deus (1854), contributed to the publication of an abundant Marian literature.”92

The coordinates of spirituality remained on the whole the established ones. Almost all of them rested on an Ignatian basis that favored asceticism, individual effort, mortification and penance and also emphasized the principle of indifference.

Also noteworthy is the wide influence of Saint Alphonsus, with a marked Eucharistic and Marian tone. Devotion to Jesus in the Blessed Sacrament was very popular, to the point of producing in Tornatore, and not only in him, a mysticism of the tabernacle that strongly promoted adoration and thus the real presence. A page illustrating his piety shows very clearly how the Lazarist Father’s day alternated continually between work and devotion to Jesus in the Blessed Sacrament.

“Devotion to the Blessed Sacrament was Mr. Tornatore’s life, for when he did not have Jesus in the sacrament he was like a dead man.

Mr. Bernardi, Priest of the Mission and fellow student of the Servant of God, told me that a few months into his novitiate this devotion was born in him, and from then on he spent all the time he had free from his duties and studies before the Blessed Sacrament.

Later, when he was a Professor, he spent his life in church before Jesus in the Sacrament.

He rose in the morning at 4 o’clock and went at once to the choir loft until the time of meditation; after meditation he said Holy Mass, and after Mass spent an hour or more in thanksgiving before the Sacrament.

Then he spent a quarter of an hour taking a little coffee, and then went to the Sacrament until a quarter of an hour before class; after class, back to the Sacrament.

After lunch, to the Sacrament.

Then he took recreation with his Confreres and, after a little rest, at about half past one went to the Sacrament, where he stayed until evening at suppertime.

After the general examination of conscience, back again to the Sacrament, where he stayed a good while longer, and then he withdrew to his room, where he prolonged his prayers and took the discipline until one o’clock after midnight.

In the years he spent at the Dal Verme house, summer and winter, he was always before the Sacrament all day long, and likewise at the College after he had stopped teaching.

When at times he was obliged to be where the Sacrament was not present he complained of it, and though he was a man who never complained, on this point he could find no peace.

To see him before the Sacrament he looked like a Seraph: with eyes closed or fixed on the Tabernacle, he remained motionless. Someone could pass by him three or four times, but there was no danger of his noticing, nor of his making the slightest movement to see who was coming and going.

One year at the College, while he was in the choir loft, the matches in his pocket caught fire.

The whole choir loft was full of smoke and stench, but he took no notice; he left when he had decided to leave, and as soon as he was outside the air fanned the flames and Mr. Tornatore was in the midst of the fire. Fortunately a Brother was passing and managed to put out the flames and so save him.

It can truly be said that when he was before the Sacrament he was dead to everything, and sometimes he had to be called and shaken before he would answer. But as a rule he never replied in the choir loft; out of respect for the Sacrament he went outside and there dealt with what he was asked.”93

No less rich in its varied expressions was Eucharistic worship, even though the nineteenth century did not develop major projects at the community level. Strong emphasis was also placed on the value of Communion, including frequent Communion, and on adoration of the Blessed Sacrament.

The rediscovery of Christ, and thus the Christ-centered character of spirituality, led to Marian piety.

The proclamation of the dogma of the Immaculate Conception and perhaps even more the apparitions of Our Lady at Lourdes in 1858 greatly stirred the consciousness of the Christian people and strengthened devotion and worship.

Together with Marian devotion, the cult of the Saints also flourished again, including devotion to Joseph, the spouse of the Virgin Mary.

Popular piety, the improvement of the clergy and of pastoral care, and above all the development of wide-ranging charitable works allow us to speak of a genuine spiritual renewal. To this both the revival of the ancient orders and the “foundation of new religious institutes, which spread very widely,” contributed considerably. “They appear as authentic signs of the presence of numerous spiritual stirrings.”94

Apart from the originality and unrepeatable character of the project the Spirit brings about in the believer’s conscience, and thus the essential novelty deriving from his inspiration, we must note the distinctive character of the spiritual framework worked out by Mother Rosa and later developed and expanded.

The charism is indeed a dynamic reality that takes shape in history and offers authentic responses to the challenges of the world.

Having discovered God’s plan through listening and searching, and having set out on the path of conversion, Rosa Gattorno consecrated herself to the Lord through the vows, worship and charity. An icon of Christ Crucified, she completed in “her flesh what is lacking in the sufferings of Jesus” through assimilation to and participation in the Mystery of the Cross, and she passed on to others her compelling spiritual experience while serving them for the love of God.

In the background stand her obedience and fidelity to the Church, her sensitivity and attentiveness to the Kairos (= event of salvation), the community dimension, the evangelizing perspective and the missionary project. Her field of action was service of the sick and so a real option for the poor and for girls in need. Her framework of reference was the scheme of the theological and cardinal virtues and the distinction between precepts and counsels.

Her manner of acting: gentleness, kindness, simplicity, a sense of motherhood.

These are some significant features of the broad spiritual project that Mother Rosa developed in faith, lived with charismatic originality, and that Father Tornatore expressed with theological competence in the Rule of 1869.

b. Sailing toward the Church

In the circular of 1876 Mother Rosa Gattorno, in Fr. Tornatore’s words, writes that the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne is God’s work, born in the Church and for the Church:

“The heavenly Father, who planted our poor Institute in the garden of his Church, looks upon it with special predilection. He has increased its houses and multiplied its members..., and with the increase of the sisters he has been pleased to strengthen it ever more in the spirit of its vocation.”

The following year, in another circular signed by her together with Fr. Tornatore, she was happy to stress the secret sympathy between Pius IX and the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne.

“He (Pius IX) has a particular affection for our Institute because our Institute was raised up by the Lord in his Church to honor in a quite special way that venerable Matron in whose womb the mystery of the Immaculate Conception of Mary was wrought, from the definition of which mystery the holy father Pius IX derives that great glory by which he shines above all popes as the sun outshines the stars. That is why our Institute, in these its beginnings, has founded and is founding the greatest number of its houses in the Pope’s state and, so to speak, around his Throne, for between the holy Father Pius IX and our Institute there is a secret sympathy.”95

Fr. Tornatore and Mother Rosa never missed an opportunity to express their fidelity to the Church and their devotion to the Vicar of Christ (Pius IX and Leo XIII).

“... The Vicar asks me about the little ship; he wants it close to him and prophesies its future to me. O my Savior! How eagerly I had run to take the little boat and bring it where the Vicar wished! But a stormy sea rises, a contrary wind rages and dashes me against a rock... After a short struggle my little ship came out more beautiful... Brought to the feet of Peter, I could say nothing to him except to ask him to say many things for me to my God: that I was bringing the little boat to the feet of his Vicar, so that it might be incorporated into his Church.”96

The image of the ship applied to the Institute is particularly eloquent and conveys well its ecclesial reality and dimension, while also bringing out the difficulty of the voyage because of the waves and storms. The goal to be reached at all costs, however, is incorporation into the Church and thus full communion with her.

Mother Rosa’s teaching is fully in harmony with the Magisterium of the Church and with the guidelines of Catholic learning.

Fr. Tornatore’s scholarly work did not neglect this fundamental element; indeed, when the storm broke over the Alberoni College and he himself was placed under investigation, he accepted it with humility and submission while waiting to clarify matters and give an account.

Likewise his apostolic activity always remained within the Church and never departed from the path traced by the Vicar of Christ and set out by the ecclesiastical Hierarchy.

This, then, is a constant! Aware that extra ecclesiam nulla salus (= outside the Church there is no salvation), an expression then upheld with a strongly apologetic emphasis, he based all his activity on dogmatic content. The Church is indeed the way of salvation the Father offers to humanity.

Fr. Tornatore would not pursue projects “almost parallel” to the life of the Church, but undertook to run the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne in collaboration and duly seeking all the necessary approvals.

His fundamental choices always matured within the Church and converged toward her. In this respect the shape of his life offers an example of sensus ecclesiae (= sense of the Church) that is still fully relevant and fresh today.

The real problems lie here. The Council made a very considerable effort and laid the foundations for an ecclesiology more in keeping with biblical, patristic, liturgical and sacramental teaching. The post-conciliar period has always reaffirmed these teachings, and the episcopates have drawn up criteria of ecclesial belonging that are an essential condition for every Christian life and every consecrated life. The solution to many problems must be sought in a sound and correct vision of the Church, just as no spiritual project can ever take off or be fruitful until it is rooted in her. Fr. Tornatore and Mother Rosa thought of the Church as a pyramid, and therefore as a strictly hierarchical structure, and showed an attachment, devotion, deference and obedience that stood every test. Moreover, their vision of faith embracing every role and every ministry, and the sacredness especially of the Vicar of Christ, the Holy See, the Bishop and the Priest, helped them to move toward the Church and so to sail toward her, making her programs their own.

The Daughters of Saint Anne are to “ask for the grace of being always united to the infallible head of the Church, the Supreme Pontiff, from whom the teaching of Jesus Christ is always received”.

In Father Tornatore we find full submission to the hierarchical Church together with a genuine ecclesial spirituality inspired by faith and deeply nourished by love.

Hence his fidelity to the Church and his defense and spreading of her teaching. All his activities matured within an ecclesial project marked by obedience to the Bishop and the Holy See.

As a good theologian he saw in painful events the condition of tribulation in which the Church community finds itself on its journey toward Christ.

c. The path of Holiness

Every religious, like every Christian, is called by virtue of baptism to holiness and to perfect union with Christ and with the Trinity.

The Rules and Constitutions of every Religious Institute form within the Church the track along which the family of the consecrated goes to God and seeks to achieve sanctification.

It is therefore necessary to look closely, and from a particular angle, at these characteristic documents in order to bring out the teaching they contain on Christian perfection and communion with God, as well as their practical provisions.

The original draft of the Rules dates from 1864 and was printed with the permission of the Bishop of Acqui. Written by Mother Rosa herself, it is wholly essential and spare. After mentioning the vows of chastity, obedience and poverty, Mother Gattorno, an eminently practical woman, speaks of “recruitment” and of the need “to increase and develop our holy Faith”. The specific activity was the care of the sick (in their homes) and the education of girls at risk.97

Noteworthy is the commitment to bring something to the sick and to serve them free of charge. Significant too is the style: to live in perfect community and poverty. This expression captures religious vocation as a whole and characterizes koinonia (= full communion) and the adoption of the Gospel standard of humility and simplicity of heart. The Mother stresses the importance of morning and evening prayer, Eucharistic Communion and union with the mystery of the Crucified.

These are indeed only a few strokes, yet from them emerge a spirit of freedom and service, an attitude of discretion, simplicity and kindness, and a strong commitment to God’s cause and to the service of the sick.

Mother Rosa, “believing at first that she saw in Mary Immaculate and Saint Francis of Assisi the models embodying her first inspiration, entrusted the Institute to their protection” and named it “Daughters of Mary Immaculate and Minims of Saint Francis of Assisi”.98

Later, however, remaining faithfully attentive to God’s will, she discovered in the figure of the holy Mother of Mary a sign of the Father’s provident love and, reassured by papal authority, gave the Institute a new face and its own spirituality:99 to offer Christ to the world, to bear witness to him as Risen and active, and to imitate concretely the models offered by the family of Our Lady.

The Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne simply proposes the sanctification common to all Christians.100

It is very interesting to note this point, rather neglected at the time, when the “category of religious” was distinguished from that of lay people and “ordinary” Christians. The text seems to anticipate the teaching of Vatican II on the universal call to holiness.

The Daughters of Saint Anne pursue this holiness by imitating Christ in the mystery of his poverty, by special devotion to Mother Saint Anne as Mother of Mary Immaculate, Mother of the Incarnate Word and Redeemer, and by practizing works of charity and mercy toward the sick, educating poor girls and teaching catechism to children.

The Constitutions of 1892, on the other hand, set aside the common vocation to perfection and holiness, emphasizing instead the personal sanctification of the members and confirming the same apostolic activities.

The vows, seen mainly as means, offer the possibility of putting on the Spirit of Jesus Christ.

Poverty, chastity and obedience free the heart to serve God, and one’s neighbor for love of him, and place the communities of the Daughters of Saint Anne on a plane of faith and charity.

The disciplinary and somewhat casuistic directives are then proposed to point out certain important observances on the spiritual journey, observances tested by experience and thus made necessary for the growth and dynamism of each member, and indirectly also of the communities and of the Institute.

The vows are God’s great gift to the Church and the sign of the presence of Christ’s Kingdom in the world. They constitute and bring about the great consecration on God’s part and enable the baptized to offer their lives to the Lord with an undivided heart.

The spiritual framework then highlights the program of the virtues. It begins with the theological virtues, in an extremely meagre, indeed almost non-existent text, in which the words faith, hope and charity do not even appear, while it stresses the need to practize them and “to seek in God and his grace that spring of living water”.101

Immediately afterward the norms indicate other virtues, first among them simplicity and prudence. Here both Tornatore’s spirituality and formation and his professional expertise come through.

On the practice of the virtues

“The daughters of Saint Anne, mindful of Our Lord’s saying, Be simple as doves and wise as serpents, will practize the virtue of simplicity with God, with their Superiors and with their neighbor, taking care that their words are the sincere expression of their thoughts, that their actions bear witness to their intention, that their outward behavior is in full accord with their spirit, and that no one is deceived by them. Moreover, at every step they will seek to be enlightened to discover where God’s will lies, the will of their Constitutions and that of their Superiors, in order to embrace it; where the true good of their neighbor lies, in order to procure it for them as far as their strength allows; and where their own harm lies, in order to avoid it. In this way they will be truly simple and prudent, that is, as Jesus Christ our Lord wants them to be.”102

Then come gentleness and humility. The Daughters of Saint Anne must learn the lesson of Christ Jesus, who says: “learn from me, for I am gentle and humble of heart”.

It points to the need to bear all insults, reproaches, persecutions and crosses, and at the same time to serve the sick and the pupils with a mother’s heart.

Endowed with modesty and straightforwardness, they cultivate freedom of spirit through detachment from relatives and friends.

Sincerely committed to religious life, the Daughters of Saint Anne constantly cultivate right intention and foster a good zeal that must permeate all their actions.

“Another means will be to flee from bitter zeal, which would make them harsh toward themselves and toward the people entrusted to their care. To give oneself up to this false zeal is a sign that in faults it is not the offense to God that displeases, nor in virtue the glory of God that pleases; rather, in the former one’s own humiliation displeases, and in the latter one’s own glory and honor pleases.”

These brief notes might suggest that Tornatore proposed a spirituality in which human effort prevails over God’s initiative, an individualistic over a communal vision, and the idea of merit over the free gift of salvation by God the Father. In fact these expressions reflect the common spiritual outlook of the second half of the last century.

This is not so in the first Rule, where the contemplation of the Holy Trinity, of Jesus and of Mary is always present in every virtue, and the sisters are told always to keep Divine Love before them, for it is he who must accomplish the art of sanctification.

Noteworthy, however, is the zeal that shines through. A zeal that seeks to maintain the religious spirit, fervor and passion for the charism within the various communities.

d. Not even a drop of coffee

“The Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate, commonly called ‘nurses’, devote themselves to the good of their neighbor in the following works: first, home nursing of the sick of both sexes, by day and by night, whatever the illness. The nurses give their care without taking anything from the sick person, not even a drop of coffee. They also take on the care of Hospitals. They always go to nurse in pairs. Second, they take poor girls at risk off the streets, that is, girls who, having no one to look after them, are in danger of losing their virtue; they educate them by having them live with them; and they also run schools for little boys up to the age of twelve.”103

This is Christian service, rooted in the work of Christ Jesus himself. He, Teacher and Lord, presents himself as the one who serves: he washes the apostles’ feet and faces passion and death for humanity.

His is a free and at the same time astonishing service, because it means sacrificing his own life, giving himself to those who insult him and drag him to the gallows. All this is humanly inconceivable and illogical, but it takes on the logic of faith and accords with the teaching of the Gospel.

It is thus a generous and committed service, responding to the needs of others in their actual situation: poor, sick, imprisoned, desperate, rejected by all. A service that takes responsibility for the other and helps through welcome, prevention and care. Think of the guarantee of a roof, a home, a safe place; think of the guarantee of support throughout the whole process of rehabilitation and reintegration into life and society.

Today the situation has changed, but “the poor you will always have with you”! Other standards will have to be adopted in doing good and helping others.

But gratuitousness and true service show no sign of fading. On the contrary, present conditions push in this direction. In this respect free service is increasingly the essential condition of Christian and religious life.

Fr. Tornatore gave a shining example and a splendid witness, and also provided, in doctrinal terms, a corresponding path of life.

“Through these works the Institute honors, among other virtues, the compassion of the Heart of Saint Anne, nursing the sick in their homes night and day; and this service must be entirely free of charge.”

The renewal so desired by Vatican II and the society of today both demand this gratuitousness.

It is the condition for carrying forward the history of Salvation, for savoring the Word of God, for presenting credibly once more the relationship between Christ and the Church, and for shaping even now the image of the Apocalypse.

The expression not even a drop of coffee simply captures the essence of the symbolic theme of gratuitousness. Here too, as elsewhere, the path moves from the concrete to the conceptual. This is the approach so often used by the Gospel and by spiritual masters, who ask that the vice of possessiveness be torn out by the roots and insist on complete detachment from goods.

But what does a drop of coffee matter? Indeed moral theology teaches that parum pro nihilo reputatur (= a small thing is counted as nothing). But what is at stake is the relationship with others, which must not be damaged for any reason and must be lived as if the service were rendered objectively to Christ. Whatever you did to one of the least of these my brothers, you did to me!

It is a matter of gratuitousness and love, of serving God with an undivided heart.

e. Promoting charity and justice

Service offered in humility and simplicity of heart, and a life lived out of compassion and accompanied by constant, persevering prayer, sweep people along, draw them in and lift them up.

Fr. Tornatore’s work in setting out in the Constitutions a program for helping the needy, the sick and girls in difficulty admirably promoted the virtue of charity. Indeed it is charity itself that urges and stimulates, confronts and renews, and cares for the needs of others as if they were the needs of Christ himself.

It is Christ, then, who calls and cries out for help in the voice of the poor and abandoned; it is Christ who begs to be comforted in the person of the afflicted and the disinherited; it is Christ who demands particular attention and sensitivity in the person of a girl who, because of her surroundings, extreme poverty or precarious conditions, might leave the way of good and take the path of evil and vice.

The impulse that comes directly from Christ Jesus works the wonders of love, spreads the Christian message like an oil stain as it penetrates human consciences, and inspires people to imitate the very gestures of charity. Moreover, the authentic standards of charity have an effect on justice and can transform the very structure of society. The program of charity and care helped people’s consciences to mature, and gradually what had been done out of charity and free of charge began to acquire legal standing. The state took it on and by legislation established a right, to health care, social assistance and education, conceived as an inalienable and universal right belonging in practice to every person.

It is therefore the community that supports, cares for and assists the sick person, providing everything necessary to restore the bodily health compromised by infirmity and illness.

In this respect charity and free service, on the purely spiritual level as on the human and social, perform acts that release extraordinary energies and considerably influence the fabric and customs of society.

In January 1877 Bishop Scalabrini issued a note presenting the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne as follows:

“At the request of Rosa Gattorno of Genoa, Foundress and Superior of the Institute called the Daughters of Saint Anne... We make known and attest the great spiritual and bodily good done in this our city and Diocese by the aforesaid Daughters of Saint Anne, whose Institute, founded in this city through the zeal and work of the aforesaid Signora Gattorno... God knows with what joy and exultation of Our heart, the fervent zeal, industrious piety and Gospel charity with which the Daughters of Saint Anne day and night assist the sick spiritually and serve them materially; clothe and feed boys and girls of every condition and, what is most important, increase the number of Religious and the good of society.”104

It will not be easy to measure this good of society! But there is no doubt that mercy, as the capacity to give one’s heart to the wretched, the attitude of compassion and the sharing with others of the Lord’s wonders, set in motion programs of transformation and wonderfully create an osmosis between charity and justice. If today the human family can enjoy the right to life, health care, social assistance and culture, this is also due to the collaboration Father Tornatore gave to Mother Rosa Gattorno, who offered shining achievements and solid witness in this field, like Saint John of God, Don Bosco and Cottolengo, thus making a decisive contribution to the fabric of society. As a result the human family has benefited greatly and has devised standards and norms de iure condendo (= law yet to be established). The life of the Daughters of Saint Anne speaks of denunciation and above all of proclamation. And so charity is wedded to justice, and together they give the world a new face.

These reflections barely allow us to cross the threshold of Giovanni Battista Tornatore’s many-sided personality and to grasp only a few elements of his spirituality.

Nor was it our intention to produce a highly scholarly work on him, still less to examine in depth his philosophical thought, with its insights and conclusions in the field of knowledge, or his theological thought and its developments. It will certainly benefit history, spirituality and the philosophical and theological sciences to undertake these studies too, as Father Gian Felice Rossi has long and commendably done.

Our main aim was to shed light on Tornatore, placing him in his proper context, highlighting only a few fundamental features of his story and relating his activity to the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne, to which he devoted his intelligence, will, mind and heart, and for which he “mortgaged” his life.

G.B. Tornatore is defined above all by this relationship with Mother Rosa Gattorno, by his spending himself, for better and for worse, for the Institute that was born, grew, developed and from a seed became a tree: a tree that never ceases to bear choice fruit for human life.

By an inscrutable design it was not given to him to rest for ever in its shade and gather all its fruit.

Adversities and even calumnies humbled him, but at the same time they tempered his life and gave him the opportunity to build up, day by day, the edifice of his spirituality.

Consecrated to God by the vows, he never turned back, and day after day he drank the bitter cup, sharing fully in the mystery of Christ who dies and rises, in the mystery of Christ Crucified.

He remained alone with his Lord, with faith in him; he persevered in every way and with great creativity in charitable projects. The many sisters he formed in the way of God and of perfection, the students of Theology to whom he generously imparted his learning, and his confreres with whom he shared the joy of community and of serving the Lord with an undivided heart, saw in him a model of life and an example. By his life Tornatore shows everyone the road to follow in order to respond positively to God’s call and to the needs of those in want.

It is the way of humility and silence, the way of simplicity and above all of compassion that Father Tornatore offers to all. His identity was built on being and never on appearing, on truth and never on diplomacy or, worse, on unclear designs and prospects. Hence his unshakeable fidelity to the Persons of the Holy Trinity, his constant adherence to the standards of the Gospel, and his obedience, veneration and devotion to the Church and in particular to the Vicar of Christ and the Holy See.

He drew strength from the Lord’s grace, from the Eucharist, from devotion to Mary and to the Saints, and faced both his inner battles and those of his relationships with others in peace and serenity, offering authoritative teaching from the chair of his own life.

Now, a century after his death (1895-1995), Father Tornatore still speaks: his hiddenness and silence are most eloquent, and his teaching and all his labors are a magnificent monument to God, to his Congregation of the Priests of the Mission, to the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne, to the Church and to the world.
